<p><b>Theresa Mary, Lady May</b> (<span class="rt-commentedText nowrap"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="&#39;t&#39; in &#39;tie&#39;">t</span><span title="/ə/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;about&#39;">ə</span><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="&#39;r&#39; in &#39;rye&#39;">r</span><span title="/iː/: &#39;ee&#39; in &#39;fleece&#39;">iː</span><span title="&#39;z&#39; in &#39;zoom&#39;">z</span><span title="/ə/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;about&#39;">ə</span></span>/</a></span></span>;<sup id="cite_ref-:3_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:3-1">&#91;1&#93;</a></sup> née <b>Brasier</b>; born 1 October 1956) is a British politician who served as <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Prime Minister of the United Kingdom">Prime Minister of the United Kingdom</a> and <a href="/wiki/Leader_of_the_Conservative_Party_(UK)" title="Leader of the Conservative Party (UK)">Leader of the Conservative Party</a> from 2016 to 2019. She previously served in <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Cabinet of the United Kingdom">cabinet</a> as <a href="/wiki/Home_Secretary" title="Home Secretary">Home Secretary</a> from 2010 to 2016, and has been <a href="/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom)" title="Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)">Member of Parliament</a> (MP) for <a href="/wiki/Maidenhead_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Maidenhead (UK Parliament constituency)">Maidenhead</a> in <a href="/wiki/Berkshire" title="Berkshire">Berkshire</a> since <a href="/wiki/1997_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="1997 United Kingdom general election">1997</a>. May was the UK's second female prime minister after <a href="/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher" title="Margaret Thatcher">Margaret Thatcher</a>, and the first woman to hold two of the <a href="/wiki/Great_Offices_of_State" title="Great Offices of State">Great Offices of State</a>. Ideologically, May identifies herself as a <a href="/wiki/One-nation_conservatism" title="One-nation conservatism">one-nation conservative</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-2">&#91;2&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May grew up in <a href="/wiki/Oxfordshire" title="Oxfordshire">Oxfordshire</a> and attended <a href="/wiki/St_Hugh%27s_College,_Oxford" title="St Hugh&#39;s College, Oxford">St Hugh's College, Oxford</a>. After graduating in 1977, she worked at the <a href="/wiki/Bank_of_England" title="Bank of England">Bank of England</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Association_for_Payment_Clearing_Services" class="mw-redirect" title="Association for Payment Clearing Services">Association for Payment Clearing Services</a>. She also served as a councillor for Durnsford in <a href="/wiki/London_Borough_of_Merton" title="London Borough of Merton">Merton</a>. After two unsuccessful attempts to be elected to the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="House of Commons of the United Kingdom">House of Commons</a>, she was elected as the MP for <a href="/wiki/Maidenhead_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Maidenhead (UK Parliament constituency)">Maidenhead</a> at the <a href="/wiki/1997_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="1997 United Kingdom general election">1997 general election</a>. From 1999 to 2010, May held several roles in <a href="/wiki/Official_Opposition_Shadow_Cabinet_(United_Kingdom)" title="Official Opposition Shadow Cabinet (United Kingdom)">shadow cabinets</a>. She was <a href="/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Conservative_Party" title="Chairman of the Conservative Party">Chairman of the Conservative Party</a> from 2002 to 2003.
</p><p>Following the <a href="/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_government_formation" title="2010 United Kingdom government formation">formation</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Cameron%E2%80%93Clegg_coalition" title="Cameron–Clegg coalition">coalition government</a> after the <a href="/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2010 United Kingdom general election">2010 general election</a>, May was appointed Home Secretary and <a href="/wiki/Minister_for_Women_and_Equalities" title="Minister for Women and Equalities">Minister for Women and Equalities</a>, giving up the latter role in 2012. Reappointed after the Conservative success in the <a href="/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2015 United Kingdom general election">2015 general election</a>, she became the longest-serving Home Secretary in over 60 years. During her <a href="/wiki/Theresa_May%27s_tenure_as_Home_Secretary" title="Theresa May&#39;s tenure as Home Secretary">tenure</a> she pursued reform of the <a href="/wiki/Police_Federation_of_England_and_Wales" title="Police Federation of England and Wales">Police Federation</a>, implemented a harder line on drugs policy including banning <a href="/wiki/Khat" title="Khat">khat</a> and brought in further <a href="/wiki/Home_Office_hostile_environment_policy" title="Home Office hostile environment policy">restrictions on immigration</a>. She oversaw the introduction of elected <a href="/wiki/Police_and_crime_commissioners" class="mw-redirect" title="Police and crime commissioners">police and crime commissioners</a>, the deportation of <a href="/wiki/Abu_Qatada_al-Filistini" title="Abu Qatada al-Filistini">Abu Qatada</a> and the creation of the <a href="/wiki/College_of_Policing" title="College of Policing">College of Policing</a> and the <a href="/wiki/National_Crime_Agency" title="National Crime Agency">National Crime Agency</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-rentoul_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rentoul-3">&#91;3&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>May supported the unsuccessful <a href="/wiki/Britain_Stronger_in_Europe" title="Britain Stronger in Europe">Britain Stronger in Europe</a> campaign for the UK to remain in the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a> (EU). She stood in the Conservative Party <a href="/wiki/2016_Conservative_Party_leadership_election" title="2016 Conservative Party leadership election">leadership election</a> to succeed Cameron, who resigned on the outcome of the <a href="/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum" title="2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum">2016 referendum</a>; she was elected and appointed Prime Minister after <a href="/wiki/Andrea_Leadsom" title="Andrea Leadsom">Andrea Leadsom</a> withdrew from the contest. She began the process of <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">withdrawing the UK from the EU</a>, triggering <a href="/wiki/Article_50_of_the_Treaty_on_European_Union" class="mw-redirect" title="Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union">Article 50</a> in March 2017. In April she announced a <a href="/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2017 United Kingdom general election">snap general election</a>, with the aims of strengthening her hand in <a href="/wiki/Brexit_negotiations" title="Brexit negotiations">Brexit negotiations</a> and highlighting her "<a href="/wiki/Strong_and_stable" title="Strong and stable">strong and stable</a>" leadership.<sup id="cite_ref-Crace_2018-07-09_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crace_2018-07-09-4">&#91;4&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5">&#91;5&#93;</a></sup> This resulted in a <a href="/wiki/Hung_parliament" title="Hung parliament">hung parliament</a> with the number of Conservative seats reduced to 317 (from 330), despite the highest vote share <a href="/wiki/1983_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="1983 United Kingdom general election">since 1983</a> and the largest increase in electoral support enjoyed by a governing party <a href="/wiki/1832_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="1832 United Kingdom general election">since 1832</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup> The loss of an overall majority prompted her to enter a <a href="/wiki/Confidence_and_supply" title="Confidence and supply">confidence and supply</a> <a href="/wiki/Conservative%E2%80%93DUP_agreement" title="Conservative–DUP agreement">arrangement</a> with the <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Unionist_Party" title="Democratic Unionist Party">Democratic Unionist Party</a> (DUP) of <a href="/wiki/Northern_Ireland" title="Northern Ireland">Northern Ireland</a> to support a <a href="/wiki/Minority_government" title="Minority government">minority government</a>.
</p><p>Following the 2017 election, May's premiership continued to be dominated by Brexit, in particular by her government's negotiations with the EU, adhering to the <a href="/wiki/Chequers_plan" title="Chequers plan">Chequers plan</a>, which led to a draft <a href="/wiki/Brexit_withdrawal_agreement" title="Brexit withdrawal agreement">Brexit withdrawal agreement</a>.  May survived two votes of no confidence in December 2018 and <a href="/wiki/2019_vote_of_confidence_in_the_May_ministry" title="2019 vote of confidence in the May ministry">January 2019</a>, but after versions of her draft withdrawal agreement were <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_votes_on_Brexit" title="Parliamentary votes on Brexit">rejected by Parliament</a> three times and her party's poor performance in the <a href="/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_local_elections" title="2019 United Kingdom local elections">local</a> and <a href="/wiki/2019_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="2019 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom">European elections in May 2019</a>, she announced her resignation later that month. She left office on 24 July and was succeeded by <a href="/wiki/Boris_Johnson" title="Boris Johnson">Boris Johnson</a>, her former <a href="/wiki/Foreign_Secretary" title="Foreign Secretary">Foreign Secretary</a>. May remains in the House of Commons as a <a href="/wiki/Backbencher" title="Backbencher">backbencher</a>.
</p><p>Other events that occurred during May's premiership included terrorist attacks in <a href="/wiki/2017_Westminster_attack" title="2017 Westminster attack">Westminster</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Manchester_Arena_bombing" title="Manchester Arena bombing">Manchester Arena</a> and <a href="/wiki/2017_London_Bridge_attack" title="2017 London Bridge attack">London Bridge</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Grenfell_Tower_fire" title="Grenfell Tower fire">Grenfell Tower fire</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Windrush_scandal" title="Windrush scandal">Windrush scandal</a>. Her government also announced a <a href="/wiki/NHS_Long_Term_Plan" title="NHS Long Term Plan">£20 billion increase in funding to the National Health Service</a>, established the first Race Disparity Audit, presided over the lowest unemployment rate since 1975,<sup id="cite_ref-ons061516_7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ons061516-7">&#91;7&#93;</a></sup> launched a 25 Year Environment Plan,<sup id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-8">&#91;8&#93;</a></sup> amending the <a href="/wiki/Climate_Change_Act_2008" title="Climate Change Act 2008">Climate Change Act 2008</a> to end the UK's contribution to global warming by 2050, passed legislation <a href="/wiki/Offensive_Weapons_Act_2019" title="Offensive Weapons Act 2019">cracking down on knife crime</a> and <a href="/wiki/Counter-Terrorism_and_Border_Security_Act_2019" title="Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019">giving extra powers to law enforcement and intelligence services to combat terrorism</a>, published the 2017 Industrial Strategy <a href="/wiki/White_Paper" class="mw-redirect" title="White Paper">White Paper</a><sup id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-9">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup> and signed an immigration treaty with <a href="/wiki/France" title="France">France</a> to stem illegal border crossings in January 2018.<sup id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10">&#91;10&#93;</a></sup> Although May did not succeed in getting much of her Brexit legislation through Parliament, her government was nevertheless responsible for passing the <a href="/wiki/European_Union_(Withdrawal)_Act_2018" title="European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018">Great Repeal Act 2018</a> and for negotiating and approving the near-entirety of the UK's <a href="/wiki/European_Union_(Withdrawal_Agreement)_Act_2020" title="European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020">terms of exit</a> from the EU.<sup id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-11">&#91;11&#93;</a></sup> As Prime Minister, May was also a prominent figure in leading the international condemnation and response to <a href="/wiki/Russia" title="Russia">Russia</a> over the <a href="/wiki/Poisoning_of_Sergei_and_Yulia_Skripal" title="Poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal">poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal</a> in March 2018.
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<h2><span id="Early_life.2C_family.2C_and_education"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_life,_family,_and_education">Early life, family, and education</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:St_Hughs_College_Oxford_-_Theresa_May_plaque.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/St_Hughs_College_Oxford_-_Theresa_May_plaque.jpg/120px-St_Hughs_College_Oxford_-_Theresa_May_plaque.jpg" decoding="async" width="120" height="164" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/St_Hughs_College_Oxford_-_Theresa_May_plaque.jpg/180px-St_Hughs_College_Oxford_-_Theresa_May_plaque.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/St_Hughs_College_Oxford_-_Theresa_May_plaque.jpg/240px-St_Hughs_College_Oxford_-_Theresa_May_plaque.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2329" data-file-height="3184" /></a><figcaption>Plaque on the room at <a href="/wiki/St_Hugh%27s_College" class="mw-redirect" title="St Hugh&#39;s College">St Hugh's College</a>, <a href="/wiki/University_of_Oxford" title="University of Oxford">University of Oxford</a> where May lived during her undergraduate studies.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Theresa May was born on 1 October 1956 in <a href="/wiki/Eastbourne" title="Eastbourne">Eastbourne</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sussex" title="Sussex">Sussex</a>. May is the only child of Zaidee Mary (<span title="Name at birth"><a href="/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names" title="Birth name">née</a></span> Barnes; 1928–1982) and Hubert Brasier (1917–1981).<sup id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-12">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup> Her father was a <a href="/wiki/Church_of_England" title="Church of England">Church of England</a> clergyman (and an <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Catholicism" title="Anglo-Catholicism">Anglo-Catholic</a>)<sup id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-13">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup> who was chaplain of an Eastbourne hospital.<sup id="cite_ref-Crockford_14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Crockford-14">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup> He later became vicar of <a href="/wiki/Enstone" title="Enstone">Enstone</a> with <a href="/wiki/Heythrop" title="Heythrop">Heythrop</a> and finally of <a href="/wiki/St_Mary_the_Virgin,_Wheatley" title="St Mary the Virgin, Wheatley">St Mary's</a> at Wheatley, to the east of Oxford.<sup id="cite_ref-Church_Times_15-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Church_Times-15">&#91;15&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup> May's mother was a supporter of the Conservative Party.<sup id="cite_ref-Theresa_May:_Iron_lady_in_waiting_18-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Theresa_May:_Iron_lady_in_waiting-18">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup> Her father died in 1981, from injuries sustained in a car accident, and her mother of <a href="/wiki/Multiple_sclerosis" title="Multiple sclerosis">multiple sclerosis</a> the following year.<sup id="cite_ref-Theresa_May_–_what_lies_beyond_the_public_image?_19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Theresa_May_–_what_lies_beyond_the_public_image?-19">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Mendick_20-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Mendick-20">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup> May later stated she was "sorry they [her parents] never saw me elected as a Member of Parliament".<sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May initially attended Heythrop Primary School, a state school in Heythrop, followed by St. Juliana's Convent School for Girls, a <a href="/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_England_and_Wales" title="Catholic Church in England and Wales">Roman Catholic</a> independent school in <a href="/wiki/Begbroke" title="Begbroke">Begbroke</a>, which closed in 1984.<sup id="cite_ref-telegraph.co.uk_22-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-telegraph.co.uk-22">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>At the age of 13, she won a place at the former Holton Park Girls' Grammar School, a state school in <a href="/wiki/Wheatley,_Oxfordshire" title="Wheatley, Oxfordshire">Wheatley</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup> During her time as a pupil, the Oxfordshire education system was reorganised, and the school became the new <a href="/wiki/Wheatley_Park_School" title="Wheatley Park School">Wheatley Park Comprehensive School</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-telegraph.co.uk_22-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-telegraph.co.uk-22">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup> May attended the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Oxford" title="University of Oxford">University of Oxford</a>, read <a href="/wiki/Geography" title="Geography">geography</a> at <a href="/wiki/St_Hugh%27s_College,_Oxford" title="St Hugh&#39;s College, Oxford">St Hugh's College</a>, and graduated with a second class <a href="/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts" title="Bachelor of Arts">BA</a> degree in 1977.<sup id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup> She was taught political geography at St Hugh's by <a href="/wiki/John_Patten,_Baron_Patten" title="John Patten, Baron Patten">John Patten, Baron Patten</a>, a future Conservative <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Education" title="Secretary of State for Education">Secretary of State for Education</a> under <a href="/wiki/John_Major" title="John Major">John Major</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>She worked at a bakery on Saturdays to earn pocket money and was a "tall, fashion-conscious young woman who from an early age spoke of her ambition to be the first woman prime minister," according to those who knew her.<sup id="cite_ref-Stamp_BBC_2016_30-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stamp_BBC_2016-30">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup> According to a university friend, Pat Frankland: "I cannot remember a time when she did not have political ambitions."<sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_career">Early career</span></h2>
<p>Between 1977 and 1983, May worked at the <a href="/wiki/Bank_of_England" title="Bank of England">Bank of England</a>, and from 1985 to 1997, at the <a href="/wiki/Association_for_Payment_Clearing_Services" class="mw-redirect" title="Association for Payment Clearing Services">Association for Payment Clearing Services</a> (APACS), as a financial consultant.<sup id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup> She served as Head of the European Affairs Unit from 1989 to 1996 and Senior Adviser on International Affairs from 1996 to 1997 in the organisation.<sup id="cite_ref-:2_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:2-33">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Entry_into_politics">Entry into politics</span></h2>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Councillor">Councillor</span></h3>
<p>May served as a councillor for Durnsford ward<sup id="cite_ref-:1_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-34">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> on the <a href="/wiki/Merton_London_Borough_Council" title="Merton London Borough Council">Borough Council</a> of the <a href="/wiki/London_Borough_of_Merton" title="London Borough of Merton">London Borough of Merton</a> from 1986 to 1994, where she was Chairman of Education (1988–1990) and Deputy Group Leader and Housing Spokesman (1992–1994).<sup id="cite_ref-:1_34-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-34">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Unsuccessful_candidacies">Unsuccessful candidacies</span></h3>
<p>In the <a href="/wiki/1992_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="1992 United Kingdom general election">1992 general election</a> May was the Conservative Party candidate for the safe Labour seat of <a href="/wiki/North_West_Durham_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="North West Durham (UK Parliament constituency)">North West Durham</a>, placing second to incumbent MP <a href="/wiki/Hilary_Armstrong" title="Hilary Armstrong">Hilary Armstrong</a>, with future Liberal Democrat leader <a href="/wiki/Tim_Farron" title="Tim Farron">Tim Farron</a> placing third.<sup id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> May then stood at the <a href="/wiki/1994_Barking_by-election" title="1994 Barking by-election">1994 Barking by-election</a>, which was prompted by the death of Labour MP <a href="/wiki/Jo_Richardson" title="Jo Richardson">Jo Richardson</a>. The seat had been continuously held by Labour since it was created in 1945, and Labour candidate <a href="/wiki/Margaret_Hodge" title="Margaret Hodge">Margaret Hodge</a> was expected to win easily, which she did. May placed a distant third.<sup id="cite_ref-mancunianmatters.co.uk_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mancunianmatters.co.uk-36">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Election">Election</span></h3>
<p>Around 18 months ahead of the <a href="/wiki/1997_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="1997 United Kingdom general election">1997 general election</a>, May was selected as the Conservative candidate for <a href="/wiki/Maidenhead_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Maidenhead (UK Parliament constituency)">Maidenhead</a>, a new seat which was created from parts of the <a href="/wiki/Safe_seat" title="Safe seat">safe</a> seats of <a href="/wiki/Windsor_and_Maidenhead_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Windsor and Maidenhead (UK Parliament constituency)">Windsor and Maidenhead</a> and <a href="/wiki/Wokingham_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Wokingham (UK Parliament constituency)">Wokingham</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:2_33-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:2-33">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> She was elected comfortably with 25,344 votes (49.8%), almost double the total of second-placed Andrew Terence Ketteringham of the Liberal Democrats, who took 13,363 votes (26.3%).<sup id="cite_ref-:0_37-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-mancunianmatters.co.uk_36-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mancunianmatters.co.uk-36">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> Despite this, her party suffered their worst defeat in over 150 years.
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_Parliamentary_career">Early Parliamentary career</span></h2>
<p>Having entered <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Parliament of the United Kingdom">Parliament</a>, May became a member of <a href="/wiki/William_Hague" title="William Hague">William Hague</a>'s front-bench <a href="/wiki/Her_Majesty%27s_Most_Loyal_Opposition_(United_Kingdom)" class="mw-redirect" title="Her Majesty&#39;s Most Loyal Opposition (United Kingdom)">Opposition</a> team, as Shadow Spokesman for Schools, Disabled People and Women (1998–1999). She became the first of the 1997 MPs to enter the Shadow Cabinet when in 1999 she was appointed Shadow Education and Employment Secretary. After the <a href="/wiki/2001_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2001 United Kingdom general election">2001 election</a> the new Conservative leader <a href="/wiki/Iain_Duncan_Smith" title="Iain Duncan Smith">Iain Duncan Smith</a> kept her in the Shadow Cabinet, moving her to the Transport portfolio.
</p><p>May was appointed the first female <a href="/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Conservative_Party" title="Chairman of the Conservative Party">Chairman of the Conservative Party</a> in July 2002. During her speech at the 2002 Conservative Party Conference, she explained why, in her view, her party must change: "You know what people call us? The Nasty Party. In recent years a number of politicians have behaved disgracefully and then compounded their offences by trying to evade responsibility. We all know who they are. Let's face it, some of them have stood on this platform."<sup id="cite_ref-Knowles2007_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Knowles2007-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Childs2008_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Childs2008-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> She accused some unnamed colleagues of trying to "make political capital out of demonising minorities", and charged others with indulging themselves "in petty feuding or sniping instead of getting behind a leader who is doing an enormous amount to change a party which has suffered two landslide defeats". She admitted that constituency selection committees seemed to prefer candidates they would "be happy to have a drink with on a Sunday morning", continuing to say, "At the last general election 38 new Tory MPs were elected. Of that total, only one was a woman and none was from an ethnic minority. Is that fair? Is one half of the population entitled to only one place out of 38?"<sup id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2003, after <a href="/wiki/Michael_Howard" title="Michael Howard">Michael Howard</a>'s election as Conservative Party and Opposition Leader in November that year, May was appointed Shadow <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Transport" title="Secretary of State for Transport">Secretary of State for Transport and the Environment</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In June 2004, she was moved to become <a href="/wiki/Shadow_Secretary_of_State_for_the_Family" title="Shadow Secretary of State for the Family">Shadow Secretary of State for the Family</a>. Following the <a href="/wiki/2005_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2005 United Kingdom general election">2005 general election</a> she was also made Shadow <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Culture,_Media_and_Sport" title="Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport">Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport</a>. After <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a> became leader, he appointed May as <a href="/wiki/Shadow_Leader_of_the_House_of_Commons" title="Shadow Leader of the House of Commons">Shadow Leader of the House of Commons</a> in December 2005 and as <a href="/wiki/Shadow_Minister_for_Women_and_Equality" class="mw-redirect" title="Shadow Minister for Women and Equality">Shadow Minister for Women and Equality</a> in July 2007. In January 2009, May was made Shadow <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Work_and_Pensions" title="Secretary of State for Work and Pensions">Secretary of State for Work and Pensions</a>.
</p><p>On 6 May 2010, May was re-elected MP for Maidenhead with an increased majority of 16,769&#160;&#8211;&#32;60% of the vote. This followed an earlier failed attempt by the Liberal Democrats to unseat her in 2005, as one of that party's leading "decapitation-strategy" targets.<sup id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Home_Secretary">Home Secretary</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Theresa_May%27s_tenure_as_Home_Secretary" title="Theresa May&#39;s tenure as Home Secretary">Theresa May's tenure as Home Secretary</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:David_Cameron%27s_visit2.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/David_Cameron%27s_visit2.jpg/170px-David_Cameron%27s_visit2.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="261" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/David_Cameron%27s_visit2.jpg/255px-David_Cameron%27s_visit2.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/David_Cameron%27s_visit2.jpg/340px-David_Cameron%27s_visit2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="461" data-file-height="709" /></a><figcaption>May with her then-leader <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a>, May 2010</figcaption></figure>
<p>On 12 May 2010, when May was appointed <a href="/wiki/Home_Secretary" title="Home Secretary">Home Secretary</a> and <a href="/wiki/Minister_for_Women_and_Equalities" title="Minister for Women and Equalities">Minister for Women and Equalities</a> by Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a> as part of his first Cabinet, she became the fourth woman to hold one of the British <a href="/wiki/Great_Offices_of_State" title="Great Offices of State">Great Offices of State</a>, after <a href="/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher" title="Margaret Thatcher">Margaret Thatcher</a> (<a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Prime Minister of the United Kingdom">Prime Minister</a>), <a href="/wiki/Margaret_Beckett" title="Margaret Beckett">Margaret Beckett</a> (<a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs" class="mw-redirect" title="Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs">Foreign Secretary</a>) and <a href="/wiki/Jacqui_Smith" title="Jacqui Smith">Jacqui Smith</a> (Home Secretary).<sup id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> As Home Secretary, May was also a member of the <a href="/wiki/National_Security_Council_(United_Kingdom)" title="National Security Council (United Kingdom)">National Security Council</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup> She was the longest-serving Home Secretary for over 60 years, since <a href="/wiki/James_Chuter_Ede" title="James Chuter Ede">James Chuter Ede</a> who served over six years and two months from August 1945 to October 1951. May's appointment as Home Secretary was somewhat unexpected, with <a href="/wiki/Chris_Grayling" title="Chris Grayling">Chris Grayling</a> having served as shadow Home Secretary in opposition.<sup id="cite_ref-Theresa_May_is_surprise_choice_to_be_Home_Secretary_45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Theresa_May_is_surprise_choice_to_be_Home_Secretary-45">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Theresa_May_is_surprise_Home_Sec_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Theresa_May_is_surprise_Home_Sec-46">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May's debut as Home Secretary involved overturning several of the previous Labour government's measures on data collection and surveillance in England and Wales. By way of a government bill which became the <a href="/wiki/Identity_Documents_Act_2010" title="Identity Documents Act 2010">Identity Documents Act 2010</a>, she brought about the abolition of the Labour government's <a href="/wiki/Identity_Cards_Act_2006" title="Identity Cards Act 2006">National Identity Card</a> and database scheme<sup id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup> and reformed the regulations on the retention of DNA samples for suspects and controls on the use of <a href="/wiki/CCTV" class="mw-redirect" title="CCTV">CCTV</a> cameras. In May 2010, May announced the adjournment of the deportation to the United States of alleged computer hacker <a href="/wiki/Gary_McKinnon" title="Gary McKinnon">Gary McKinnon</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> She also suspended the registration scheme for carers of children and vulnerable people, with May saying that the measures were "draconian. You were assumed to be guilty until you were proven innocent, and told you were able to work with children."<sup id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup> On 4 August 2010, it was reported that May was scrapping the former Labour government's proposed "go orders" scheme to protect women from <a href="/wiki/Domestic_violence" title="Domestic violence">domestic violence</a> by banning abusers from the victim's home.<sup id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In June 2010, May faced her first major national security incident as Home Secretary with the <a href="/wiki/Cumbria_shootings" title="Cumbria shootings">Cumbria shootings</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> She delivered her first major speech in the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="House of Commons of the United Kingdom">House of Commons</a> as Home Secretary in a statement on this incident,<sup id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup> later visiting the victims with the Prime Minister.<sup id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> Also in June 2010, May banned the Indian Muslim preacher <a href="/wiki/Zakir_Naik" title="Zakir Naik">Zakir Naik</a> from entering the United Kingdom.<sup id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to <i>The Daily Telegraph</i>, a Home Office official who disagreed with this decision was suspended.<sup id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-59">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup> In late June 2010, May announced plans for a temporary cap on UK visas for non-EU migrants.<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup> The move raised concerns about the impact on the British economy.<sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In August 2013, May supported the detention of <a href="/wiki/David_Miranda_(politician)" title="David Miranda (politician)">David Miranda</a>, partner of <i>Guardian</i> journalist <a href="/wiki/Glenn_Greenwald" title="Glenn Greenwald">Glenn Greenwald</a>, under the <a href="/wiki/Terrorism_Act_2000" title="Terrorism Act 2000">Terrorism Act 2000</a>, saying that critics of the Metropolitan Police action needed to "think about what they are condoning".<sup id="cite_ref-miranda_62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-miranda-62">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup> Lib Dem peer and former Director of Public Prosecutions <a href="/wiki/Ken_Macdonald" title="Ken Macdonald">Ken Macdonald</a> accused May of an "ugly and unhelpful" attempt to implicate those who were concerned about the police action of "condoning terrorism".<sup id="cite_ref-miranda_62-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-miranda-62">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup> The High Court subsequently acknowledged there were "indirect implications for press freedom" but ruled the detention legal.<sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup> A 2016 ruling by the <a href="/wiki/Court_of_Appeal_(England_and_Wales)" title="Court of Appeal (England and Wales)">Court of Appeal</a> found that the provision of the Terrorism Act used for Miranda's detention was "incompatible with the <a href="/wiki/European_Convention_on_Human_Rights" title="European Convention on Human Rights">European convention on human rights</a>", but that the detention itself was lawful.<sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May also championed legislation popularly dubbed the <a href="/wiki/Investigatory_Powers_Bill" class="mw-redirect" title="Investigatory Powers Bill">Snooper's Charter</a>, requiring internet and mobile service providers to keep records of internet usage, voice calls, messages and email for up to a year in case police requested access to the records while investigating a crime. The Liberal Democrats had blocked the <a href="/wiki/Draft_Communications_Data_Bill" title="Draft Communications Data Bill">first attempt</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup> but after the Conservative Party obtained a majority in the 2015 general election May announced a new <a href="/wiki/Draft_Investigatory_Powers_Bill" class="mw-redirect" title="Draft Investigatory Powers Bill">Draft Investigatory Powers Bill</a> similar to the Draft Communications Data Bill, although with more limited powers and additional oversight.<sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Police_and_crime">Police and crime</span></h3>
<p>Speaking at the <a href="/wiki/Association_of_Chief_Police_Officers" title="Association of Chief Police Officers">Association of Chief Police Officers</a> (ACPO) conference in June 2010, May announced radical cuts to the Home Office budget, likely to lead to a reduction in police numbers.<sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup> In July 2010, May presented the House of Commons with proposals for a fundamental review of the previous Labour government's security and counter-terrorism legislation, including "stop and search" powers, and her intention to review the 28-day limit on detaining terrorist suspects without charge.<sup id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-70">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-71">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In July 2010, May announced a package of reforms to policing in England and Wales in the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="House of Commons of the United Kingdom">House of Commons</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Shakeup_72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Shakeup-72">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup> The previous Labour Government's central crime agency, <a href="/wiki/Serious_Organised_Crime_Agency" title="Serious Organised Crime Agency">Soca (Serious Organised Crime Agency)</a>, was to be replaced by a new <a href="/wiki/National_Crime_Agency" title="National Crime Agency">National Crime Agency</a>. In common with the Conservative Party 2010 general election manifesto's flagship proposal for a "<a href="/wiki/Big_Society" title="Big Society">Big Society</a>" based on voluntary action, May also proposed increasing the role of civilian "reservists" for crime control. The reforms were rejected by the Opposition <a href="/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK)" title="Labour Party (UK)">Labour Party</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Shakeup_72-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Shakeup-72">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following the actions of some members of <a href="/wiki/Black_Bloc" class="mw-redirect" title="Black Bloc">Black Bloc</a> in vandalising allegedly <a href="/wiki/UK_Uncut" title="UK Uncut">tax-avoiding</a> shops and businesses on the day of the March 2011 TUC march, the Home Secretary unveiled reforms<sup id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-73">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> curbing the right to protest, including giving police extra powers to remove masked individuals and to police social networking sites to prevent <a href="/wiki/Public_Order_Act_1986" title="Public Order Act 1986">illegal protest</a> without police consent or notification.<sup id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2012, despite inquiries by both <a href="/wiki/Scotland_Yard" title="Scotland Yard">Scotland Yard</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Independent_Police_Complaints_Commission" title="Independent Police Complaints Commission">Independent Police Complaints Commission</a> ruling that there was no new evidence to warrant further investigation, after discussions with <a href="/wiki/Doreen_Lawrence" title="Doreen Lawrence">Doreen Lawrence</a>, May commissioned <a href="/wiki/Mark_Ellison" title="Mark Ellison">Mark Ellison</a> to review Scotland Yard's investigations into alleged police corruption.<sup id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-75">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup> The report was presented to Parliament by May on 6 March 2014. <a href="/wiki/Bernard_Hogan-Howe" class="mw-redirect" title="Bernard Hogan-Howe">Sir Bernard Hogan-Howe</a>, <a href="/wiki/Commissioner_of_the_Metropolitan_Police" class="mw-redirect" title="Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police">Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police</a> said the report, which has prompted an inquiry into undercover policing, was "devastating".<sup id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-76">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In July 2013, May welcomed the fact that crime had fallen by more than 10% under the coalition government, while still being able to make savings. She said that this was partly due to the government removing red tape and scrapping targets to allow the police to concentrate on crime-fighting.<sup id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-77">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2014, May delivered a speech to the <a href="/wiki/Police_Federation_of_England_and_Wales" title="Police Federation of England and Wales">Police Federation</a>, in which she criticised aspects of the culture of the police force.<sup id="cite_ref-May_tells_police_–_change_or_be_changed_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-May_tells_police_–_change_or_be_changed-78">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup> In the speech, she said:
</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r996844942">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em 0;padding:0 40px}.mw-parser-output .templatequote .templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;padding-left:1.6em;margin-top:0}</style><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>When you remember the list of recent revelations about police misconduct, it is not enough to mouth platitudes about "a few bad apples". The problem might lie with a minority of officers, but it is still a significant problem and a problem that needs to be addressed ... according to one survey carried out recently, only 42% of black people from a Caribbean background trust the police. That is simply not sustainable ... I will soon publish proposals to strengthen the protections available to whistleblowers in the police. I am creating a new criminal offence of police corruption. And I am determined that the use of stop and search must come down, become more targeted and lead to more arrests.<sup id="cite_ref-2014_Police_Federation_speech_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2014_Police_Federation_speech-79">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>On 9 December 2010, in the wake of violent <a href="/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_student_protests" title="2010 United Kingdom student protests">student demonstrations</a> in central London against increases to higher-education <a href="/wiki/Tuition_fees_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Tuition fees in the United Kingdom">tuition fees</a>, May praised the actions of the police in controlling the demonstrations but was described by <i><a href="/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph" title="The Daily Telegraph">The Daily Telegraph</a></i> as "under growing political pressure" due to her handling of the protests.<sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-81">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In December 2010, May declared that deployment of water cannon by police forces in mainland Britain was an operational decision which had been "resisted until now by senior police officers."<sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup> She rejected their use following the <a href="/wiki/2011_England_riots" title="2011 England riots">widespread rioting in summer 2011</a> and said: "the way we police in Britain is not through use of water cannon. The way we police in Britain is through consent of communities." May said: "I condemn utterly the violence in Tottenham... Such disregard for public safety and property will not be tolerated, and the Metropolitan Police have my full support in restoring order."<sup id="cite_ref-patrol-streets_83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-patrol-streets-83">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the aftermath of the riots May urged the identification of as many as possible of the young criminals involved. She said: "when I was in Manchester last week, the issue was raised to me about the anonymity of juveniles who are found guilty of crimes of this sort. The Crown Prosecution Service is to order prosecutors to apply for anonymity to be lifted in any youth case they think is in the public interest. The law currently protects the identity of any suspect under the age of 18, even if they are convicted, but it also allows for an application to have such restrictions lifted, if deemed appropriate." May added that "what I've asked for is that CPS guidance should go to prosecutors to say that where possible, they should be asking for the anonymity of juveniles who are found guilty of criminal activity to be lifted".<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Anti-social_behaviour">Anti-social behaviour</span></h4>
<p>In July 2010, May proposed to review the previous <a href="/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK)" title="Labour Party (UK)">Labour</a> Government's <a href="/wiki/Anti-social_behaviour" title="Anti-social behaviour">anti-social behaviour</a> legislation signalling the abolition of the "<a href="/wiki/Asbo" class="mw-redirect" title="Asbo">Anti-Social Behaviour Order</a>" (ASBO). She identified the policy's high level of failure with almost half of ASBOs breached between 2000 and 2008, leading to "fast-track" criminal convictions. May proposed a less punitive, community-based approach to tackling social disorder. May suggested that anti-social behaviour policy "must be turned on its head", reversing the ASBO's role as the flagship crime control policy legislation under Labour.<sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup> Former Labour Home Secretaries <a href="/wiki/David_Blunkett" title="David Blunkett">David Blunkett</a> (who introduced ASBOs) and <a href="/wiki/Alan_Johnson" title="Alan Johnson">Alan Johnson</a> expressed their disapproval of the proposals.<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Drug_policy">Drug policy</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Deakhat.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Deakhat.jpg/220px-Deakhat.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="142" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Deakhat.jpg/330px-Deakhat.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Deakhat.jpg/440px-Deakhat.jpg 2x" data-file-width="496" data-file-height="320" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Khat" title="Khat">Khat</a> bundles</figcaption></figure>
<p>In July 2013, May decided to ban the stimulant <a href="/wiki/Khat" title="Khat">khat</a>, against the advice of the <a href="/wiki/Advisory_Council_on_the_Misuse_of_Drugs" title="Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs">Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs</a> (ACMD). The council reached the conclusion that there was "insufficient evidence" it caused health problems.<sup id="cite_ref-88" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> Explaining the change in the classification May said: "The decision to bring khat under control is finely balanced and takes into account the expert scientific advice and these broader concerns", and pointed out that the product had already been banned in the majority of other EU member states, as well as most of the G8 countries including Canada and the US.<sup id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> A report on khat use by the ACMD published in January 2013 had noted the product had been associated with "acute psychotic episodes", "chronic liver disease" and family breakdown. However, it concluded that there is no risk of harm for most users, and recommended that khat remain uncontrolled due to lack of evidence for these associations.<sup id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-90">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Liberal Democrat minister <a href="/wiki/Norman_Baker" title="Norman Baker">Norman Baker</a> accused May of suppressing proposals to treat rather than prosecute minor drug offenders from a report into drug policy commissioned by the Home Office.<sup id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> The Home Office denied that its officials had considered this as part of their strategy. Baker cited difficulties in working with May as the reason for his resignation from the Home Office in the run-up to the 2015 general election.<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-94">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-96">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Immigration">Immigration</span></h3>
<p>In 2010, May promised to bring the level of net migration down to less than 100,000.<sup id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup> <i>The Independent</i> reported in February 2015, "The <a href="/wiki/Office_for_National_Statistics" title="Office for National Statistics">Office for National Statistics</a> (ONS) announced a net flow of 298,000 migrants to the UK in the 12 months to September 2014—up from 210,000 in the previous year."<sup id="cite_ref-migration_98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-migration-98">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup> In total, 624,000 people <a href="/wiki/Modern_immigration_to_the_United_Kingdom" title="Modern immigration to the United Kingdom">migrated to the UK</a> in the year ending September 2014 and 327,000 left in the same period. Statistics showed "significant increases in migration among both non-EU citizens—up 49,000 to 292,000—and EU citizens, which rose by 43,000 to 251,000."<sup id="cite_ref-migration_98-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-migration-98">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In May 2012 she told the <i><a href="/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph" title="The Daily Telegraph">Daily Telegraph</a></i> of her intention "to create here in Britain a <a href="/wiki/Home_Office_hostile_environment_policy" title="Home Office hostile environment policy">really hostile environment</a> for illegal migration".<sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May rejected the European Union's proposal of <a href="/wiki/European_migrant_crisis#Relocation_and_resettlement_of_asylum_seekers" class="mw-redirect" title="European migrant crisis">compulsory refugee quotas</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup> She said that it was important to help people living in war-zone regions and refugee camps but "not the ones who are strong and rich enough to come to Europe".<sup id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> In May 2016, <i>The Daily Telegraph</i> reported that she had tried to save £4m by rejecting an intelligence project to use aircraft surveillance to detect illegal immigrant boats.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Family_migration">Family migration</span></h4>
<p>In June 2012, Theresa May announced that new restrictions would be introduced to reduce the number of non-<a href="/wiki/European_Economic_Area" title="European Economic Area">European Economic Area</a> family migrants. The changes were mostly intended to apply to new applicants after 9 July 2012.<sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The newly introduced rules came into effect on 9 July 2012 allowing only those British citizens earning more than £18,600 to bring their spouses or their children to live with them in the UK. This figure would rise significantly in cases where visa applications are also made for children. They also increased the current two-year probationary period for partners to 5 years. The rules also prevent any adult and elderly dependents from settling in the UK unless they can demonstrate that, as a result of age, <a href="/wiki/Illness" class="mw-redirect" title="Illness">illness</a> or <a href="/wiki/Disability" title="Disability">disability</a>, they require a level of long-term personal care that can only be provided by a relative in the UK.<sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/House_of_Lords" title="House of Lords">House of Lords</a> was concerned about the immigration issue and therefore addressed the PM in Parliament as to whether she had examined the impact on communities and families on modest incomes, but it received no direct response.<sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup> The human rights group <a href="/wiki/Liberty_(advocacy_group)" title="Liberty (advocacy group)">Liberty</a> concluded that the new rules showed scant regard to the impact they would have on genuine families.<sup id="cite_ref-Liberty_briefing_106-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Liberty_briefing-106">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/All-Party_Parliamentary_Group" class="mw-redirect" title="All-Party Parliamentary Group">All-Party Parliamentary Group</a> on Migration conducted an evidence based inquiry into the impact of the rules and concluded in their report that the rules were causing very young children to be separated from their parents and could exile <a href="/wiki/British_citizen" class="mw-redirect" title="British citizen">British citizens</a> from the UK.<sup id="cite_ref-AAPG_report_107-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AAPG_report-107">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Deportation_decisions">Deportation decisions</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Memorandum_of_Understanding_on_transnational_crime_(5937407114).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Memorandum_of_Understanding_on_transnational_crime_%285937407114%29.jpg/220px-Memorandum_of_Understanding_on_transnational_crime_%285937407114%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Memorandum_of_Understanding_on_transnational_crime_%285937407114%29.jpg/330px-Memorandum_of_Understanding_on_transnational_crime_%285937407114%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Memorandum_of_Understanding_on_transnational_crime_%285937407114%29.jpg/440px-Memorandum_of_Understanding_on_transnational_crime_%285937407114%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2136" data-file-height="1424" /></a><figcaption>May, David Cameron and <a href="/wiki/Najib_Razak" title="Najib Razak">Najib Razak</a>, 14 July 2011</figcaption></figure>
<p>At the Conservative Party Conference in October 2011, while arguing that the Human Rights Act needed to be amended, May gave the example of a foreign national who the Courts ruled was allowed to remain in the UK, "because—and I am not making this up—he had a pet cat". In response, the Royal Courts of Justice issued a statement, denying that this was the reason for the tribunal's decision in that case, and stating that the real reason was that he was in a genuine relationship with a British partner, and owning a pet cat was simply one of many pieces of evidence given to show that the relationship was "genuine". The Home Office had failed to apply its own rules for dealing with unmarried partners of people settled in the UK.<sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup> Amnesty International said May's comments only fuelled "myths and misconceptions" about the Human Rights Act and Justice Secretary <a href="/wiki/Kenneth_Clarke" title="Kenneth Clarke">Kenneth Clarke</a> subsequently called May's comments "laughable and childlike."<sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In June 2012, May was found in <a href="/wiki/Contempt_of_court" title="Contempt of court">contempt of court</a> by Judge Barry Cotter, and stood accused of "totally unacceptable and regrettable behaviour", being said to have shown complete disregard for a legal agreement to free an Algerian from a UK Immigration Detention Centre. As she eventually allowed the prisoner to be freed, May avoided further sanctions including fines or imprisonment.<sup id="cite_ref-telegraph1_111-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-telegraph1-111">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ukimmigrationbarristers1_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ukimmigrationbarristers1-112">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May responded to a Supreme Court decision in November 2013 to overturn her predecessor <a href="/wiki/Jacqui_Smith" title="Jacqui Smith">Jacqui Smith</a>'s revocation of Iraqi-born terror suspect Al Jedda's British citizenship by ordering it to be revoked for a second time, making him the first person to be stripped twice of British citizenship.<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May was accused by <a href="/wiki/Roger_Roberts,_Baron_Roberts_of_Llandudno" title="Roger Roberts, Baron Roberts of Llandudno">Lord Roberts</a> of being willing to allow someone to die "to score a political point" over the deportation of mentally ill Nigerian man Isa Muazu.<sup id="cite_ref-Gdn20131129_116-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gdn20131129-116">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> According to Muazu's solicitor, May had arranged for the asylum seeker, who was said to be "near death" after a 100-day hunger strike, to be deported by a chartered private jet.<sup id="cite_ref-Gdn20131129_116-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gdn20131129-116">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> To strengthen the Home Office's tough stance, an "end of life" plan was reportedly offered to Muazu, who was one of a number of hunger strikers at the <a href="/wiki/Harmondsworth_Immigration_Removal_Centre" title="Harmondsworth Immigration Removal Centre">Harmondsworth Immigration Removal Centre</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Abu_Qatada_deportation">Abu Qatada deportation</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Abu_Qatada_boards_plane.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Abu_Qatada_boards_plane.jpg/220px-Abu_Qatada_boards_plane.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="151" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Abu_Qatada_boards_plane.jpg/330px-Abu_Qatada_boards_plane.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Abu_Qatada_boards_plane.jpg/440px-Abu_Qatada_boards_plane.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3600" data-file-height="2463" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Abu_Qatada_al-Filistini" title="Abu Qatada al-Filistini">Abu Qatada</a>'s deportation to Jordan in July 2013</figcaption></figure>
<p>On 7 July 2013, <a href="/wiki/Abu_Qatada_al-Filistini" title="Abu Qatada al-Filistini">Abu Qatada</a>, a radical cleric arrested in 2002, was deported to <a href="/wiki/Jordan" title="Jordan">Jordan</a> after a decade-long battle that had cost the nation £1.7 million in legal fees,<sup id="cite_ref-The_Guardian_118-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-The_Guardian-118">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup> and several prior Home Secretaries had not resolved.<sup id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-119">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup> The deportation was the result of a treaty negotiated by May in April 2013, under which Jordan agreed to give Qatada a fair trial, by not using evidence that may have been obtained against him through torture.<sup id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-120">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May pointed to Qatada's deportation as a triumph, guaranteeing in September 2013 that "he will not be returning to the <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom" title="United Kingdom">UK</a>", and declaring in her 2016 leadership campaign announcement that she was told that she "couldn't deport Abu Qatada" but that she "flew to Jordan and negotiated the treaty that got him out of Britain for good".<sup id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-121">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-rentoul_3-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rentoul-3">&#91;3&#93;</a></sup> The Qatada deportation also shaped May's views on the <a href="/wiki/European_Convention_on_Human_Rights" title="European Convention on Human Rights">European Convention on Human Rights</a> and <a href="/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights" title="European Court of Human Rights">European Court of Human Rights</a>, saying that they had "moved the goalposts" and had a "crazy interpretation of our human rights laws", as a result, May has since campaigned against the institutions, saying that British withdrawal from them should be considered.<sup id="cite_ref-The_Guardian_118-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-The_Guardian-118">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id=".22Go_Home.22_advertisements"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="&quot;Go_Home&quot;_advertisements">"Go Home" advertisements</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/%22Go_Home%22_vans" title="&quot;Go Home&quot; vans">"Go Home" vans</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1066479718"><table class="infobox" style="width: 250px; float: right; clear: right; margin:0 0 1.5em 1.5em"><tbody><tr><th colspan="2" class="infobox-above" style="font-size:115%">External image</th></tr><tr><td colspan="2" class="infobox-full-data" style="text-align: left"><span typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="image icon" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/61/Searchtool.svg/16px-Searchtool.svg.png" decoding="async" width="16" height="16" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/61/Searchtool.svg/24px-Searchtool.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/61/Searchtool.svg/32px-Searchtool.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="512" data-file-height="512" /></span></span> <a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://static.independent.co.uk/s3fs-public/styles/story_large/public/thumbnails/image/2013/07/31/11/immigration.jpg">Image of the "Go Home" advert vans</a>. From <i><a href="/wiki/The_Independent" title="The Independent">The Independent</a></i>, Credit: Home Office/PA.</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>In August 2013, the Home Office engaged in an advertising campaign directed at illegal immigrants.<sup id="cite_ref-122" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-122">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup> The advertisements, in the form of mobile advertising hoardings on the back of lorries, told illegal immigrants to "go home or face arrest", with an image of a person in handcuffs, and were deployed in six London boroughs with substantial ethnic minority populations. They were widely criticised as creating a <a href="/wiki/Home_Office_hostile_environment_policy" title="Home Office hostile environment policy">hostile atmosphere</a> for members of ethnic minority groups.<sup id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-123">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup> The shadow Home Secretary, <a href="/wiki/Yvette_Cooper" title="Yvette Cooper">Yvette Cooper</a>, described their language as being reminiscent of that used by the <a href="/wiki/National_Front_(UK)" title="National Front (UK)">National Front</a> in the 1970s.<sup id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-124">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup> An adjudication by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said that "the claim [that 106 arrests were made last week] was misleading and had not been substantiated" was followed by the advertisements being withdrawn after being banned by the ASA.<sup id="cite_ref-125" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-125">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Passport_backlog">Passport backlog</span></h4>
<p>In mid 2014, the Passport Office faced a backlog in developing processing passport applications, with around 30,000 applications hit by delays.<sup id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-126">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup> David Cameron suggested this had come about due to the Passport Office's receiving an "above normal" 300,000-rise in applications.<sup id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-127">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup> It was revealed, however, that May had been warned the year before, in July 2013, that a surge of 350,000 extra applications could occur owing to the closure of processing overseas under Chancellor Osborne's programme of cuts.<sup id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-128">&#91;128&#93;</a></sup> Around £674,000 was paid to staff who helped clear the backlog.<sup id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-129">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Windrush_scandal">Windrush scandal</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Windrush_scandal" title="Windrush scandal">Windrush scandal</a></div>
<p>In April 2018, May's <a href="/wiki/Home_Office_hostile_environment_policy" title="Home Office hostile environment policy">hostile environment policy</a> became the focus of British politics in what came to be known as the <a href="/wiki/Windrush_scandal" title="Windrush scandal">Windrush scandal</a>, in which members of the <a href="/wiki/Windrush_generation" class="mw-redirect" title="Windrush generation">Windrush generation</a> of Afro-Caribbean Britons were threatened with deportation by the Home Office and in at least 83 cases, illegally deported from the UK.<sup id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-130">&#91;130&#93;</a></sup>  The policy also affected the lives of many thousands of people who were in the United Kingdom legally by causing them to be sacked from employment,<sup id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-131">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup> preventing access to health care, illegally demanding money,<sup id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-132">&#91;132&#93;</a></sup> exiling them and preventing their return to the UK,<sup id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-133">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup> and leaving them destitute. The scandal led to the resignation of May's successor Amber Rudd as Home Secretary,<sup id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-134">&#91;134&#93;</a></sup>  and her replacement by <a href="/wiki/Sajid_Javid" title="Sajid Javid">Sajid Javid</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-135">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup> Responding to questions in Parliament on the Windrush scandal on 25 April, May maintained that the hostile environment policy would remain government policy.<sup id="cite_ref-136" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-136">&#91;136&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Birmingham_schools_row">Birmingham schools row</span></h3>
<p>In June 2014, an inflamed public argument arose between Home Office and <a href="/wiki/Department_for_Education" title="Department for Education">Education</a> Ministers about responsibility for <a href="/wiki/Operation_Trojan_Horse" class="mw-redirect" title="Operation Trojan Horse">alleged extremism in Birmingham schools</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-telegraph-20140604bb_137-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-telegraph-20140604bb-137">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-telegraph-20140604ty_138-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-telegraph-20140604ty-138">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup> Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a> intervened to resolve the row, insisting that May sack her <a href="/wiki/Special_advisers_(UK_government)" class="mw-redirect" title="Special advisers (UK government)">Special Advisor</a> <a href="/wiki/Fiona_McLeod_Hill" class="mw-redirect" title="Fiona McLeod Hill">Fiona Cunningham</a> (now Hill) for releasing on May's website a confidential letter to May's colleagues,<sup id="cite_ref-139" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-139">&#91;139&#93;</a></sup> and that <a href="/wiki/Michael_Gove" title="Michael Gove">Michael Gove</a>, the Education Secretary, apologise to the Home Office's <a href="/wiki/Office_for_Security_and_Counter-Terrorism" title="Office for Security and Counter-Terrorism">head of Security and Counter-Terrorism</a>, <a href="/wiki/Charles_Farr_(civil_servant)" title="Charles Farr (civil servant)">Charles Farr</a>, for uncomplimentary briefings of him appearing on the front page of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Times" title="The Times">The Times</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-bbc-20140608_140-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbc-20140608-140">&#91;140&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-observer-20140607_141-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-observer-20140607-141">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Minister_for_Women_and_Equalities">Minister for Women and Equalities</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theresa_May_and_Justine_Greening_speaking_at_-YouthForChange_(14503114089).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Theresa_May_and_Justine_Greening_speaking_at_-YouthForChange_%2814503114089%29.jpg/220px-Theresa_May_and_Justine_Greening_speaking_at_-YouthForChange_%2814503114089%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Theresa_May_and_Justine_Greening_speaking_at_-YouthForChange_%2814503114089%29.jpg/330px-Theresa_May_and_Justine_Greening_speaking_at_-YouthForChange_%2814503114089%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Theresa_May_and_Justine_Greening_speaking_at_-YouthForChange_%2814503114089%29.jpg/440px-Theresa_May_and_Justine_Greening_speaking_at_-YouthForChange_%2814503114089%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1728" /></a><figcaption>May and <a href="/wiki/Justine_Greening" title="Justine Greening">Justine Greening</a> speaking at <i>Youth For Change</i>, 19 July 2014</figcaption></figure>
<p>May held the office of <a href="/wiki/Minister_for_Women_and_Equalities" title="Minister for Women and Equalities">Minister for Women and Equalities</a> in parallel to her office of Home Secretary from 2010 to September 2012, when this role was taken over by <a href="/wiki/Maria_Miller" title="Maria Miller">Maria Miller</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-gran04sep12_142-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-gran04sep12-142">&#91;142&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May's appointment as Minister for Women and Equalities was controversial, and was met with criticism by many in the <a href="/wiki/LGBT_community" title="LGBT community">LGBT community</a><sup id="cite_ref-143" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-143">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-144" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-144">&#91;144&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-145" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-145">&#91;145&#93;</a></sup> due to May's record of consistently opposing <a href="/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="LGBT rights in the United Kingdom">LGBT rights</a> from 1997 to 2004:<sup id="cite_ref-146" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-146">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup> she voted against equalising the age of consent in 1998, she spoke in favour of <a href="/wiki/Section_28" title="Section 28">Section 28</a> in 2001,<sup id="cite_ref-147" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-147">&#91;147&#93;</a></sup> and she spoke against greater <a href="/wiki/LGBT_adoption" class="mw-redirect" title="LGBT adoption">adoption rights for homosexuals</a> in 2002.<sup id="cite_ref-148" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-148">&#91;148&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-149" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-149">&#91;149&#93;</a></sup> May later stated, during an appearance on the BBC's <i><a href="/wiki/Question_Time_(TV_series)" class="mw-redirect" title="Question Time (TV series)">Question Time</a></i> in 2010, that she had "changed her mind" on gay adoption.<sup id="cite_ref-150" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-150">&#91;150&#93;</a></sup> Writing for <i><a href="/wiki/PinkNews" title="PinkNews">PinkNews</a></i> in June 2010, May detailed proposals for improving LGBT rights including measures to tackle homophobia in sport, advocating British society's need for "cultural change".<sup id="cite_ref-151" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-151">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 2 July 2010, May stated she would be supporting the previous Labour Government's Anti-Discrimination Laws enshrined in the <a href="/wiki/Equality_Act_2010" title="Equality Act 2010">Equality Act 2010</a> despite having previously opposed it.<sup id="cite_ref-152" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-152">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup> The Equality Act came into effect in England, Wales and Scotland on 1 October 2010.<sup id="cite_ref-153" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-153">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup> She did however announce that a clause she dubbed "<a href="/wiki/Harriet_Harman" title="Harriet Harman">Harman</a>'s Law"<sup id="cite_ref-154" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-154">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup> which would have required <a href="/wiki/Non-departmental_public_body" title="Non-departmental public body">public bodies</a> to consider how they can reduce socio-economic inequalities when making decisions about spending and services<sup id="cite_ref-155" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-155">&#91;155&#93;</a></sup> would be scrapped on the grounds that it was "unworkable".<sup id="cite_ref-156" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-156">&#91;156&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Prime_Minister_.282016.E2.80.932019.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Prime_Minister_(2016–2019)">Prime Minister (2016–2019)</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Premiership_of_Theresa_May" title="Premiership of Theresa May">Premiership of Theresa May</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Leadership_election">Leadership election</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK)_leadership_election,_2016" class="mw-redirect" title="Conservative Party (UK) leadership election, 2016">Conservative Party (UK) leadership election, 2016</a></div>
<p>On 30 June 2016, May announced her candidacy for the leadership of the Conservative Party to replace <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a>, who resigned following the outcome of the <a href="/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum" title="2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum">European Union membership referendum</a> in which 52% of voters voted in favour of leaving the EU. May emphasised the need for unity within the party regardless of positions on leaving the EU, saying she could bring "strong leadership" and a "positive vision" for the country's future. Despite having backed a vote to remain in the EU, she insisted that there would be no second referendum, saying: "The campaign was fought... and the public gave their verdict. There must be no attempts to remain inside the EU, no attempts to rejoin it through the back door... Brexit means Brexit". An opinion poll that day found 47% of people choosing May as their preferred candidate to be prime minister.<sup id="cite_ref-157" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-157">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup>
