</p><p>May's supporters included a number of Cabinet ministers, such as <a href="/wiki/Amber_Rudd" title="Amber Rudd">Amber Rudd</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chris_Grayling" title="Chris Grayling">Chris Grayling</a>, <a href="/wiki/Justine_Greening" title="Justine Greening">Justine Greening</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jeremy_Hunt" title="Jeremy Hunt">Jeremy Hunt</a>, <a href="/wiki/Michael_Fallon" title="Michael Fallon">Michael Fallon</a> and <a href="/wiki/Patrick_McLoughlin" title="Patrick McLoughlin">Patrick McLoughlin</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-158" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-158">&#91;158&#93;</a></sup> She received the most votes in the first round of voting on 5 July, receiving support from 165 MPs, with rivals <a href="/wiki/Andrea_Leadsom" title="Andrea Leadsom">Andrea Leadsom</a> receiving 66 votes and <a href="/wiki/Michael_Gove" title="Michael Gove">Michael Gove</a> 48.<sup id="cite_ref-159" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-159">&#91;159&#93;</a></sup> The two candidates with the fewest votes, <a href="/wiki/Liam_Fox" title="Liam Fox">Liam Fox</a> and <a href="/wiki/Stephen_Crabb" title="Stephen Crabb">Stephen Crabb</a>, immediately announced their support for May.<sup id="cite_ref-160" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-160">&#91;160&#93;</a></sup> May came in first place in the second ballot on 7 July with an overwhelming majority of 199 MPs, compared with 84 for Leadsom and 46 for Gove, who was eliminated.<sup id="cite_ref-161" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-161">&#91;161&#93;</a></sup> Afterwards, May stated that she was delighted with her support among MPs, and she progressed to a vote of the Conservative Party membership against Leadsom.<sup id="cite_ref-162" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-162">&#91;162&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 11 July, Leadsom announced her withdrawal from the leadership contest hours after May had made her first official campaign speech, saying her lack of support amongst Conservative MPs compared to May would be too great a hindrance to becoming a credible prime minister.<sup id="cite_ref-163" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-163">&#91;163&#93;</a></sup> As the sole remaining candidate, May was formally declared Leader of the Conservative Party that evening.<sup id="cite_ref-wednesday_164-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wednesday-164">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-165" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-165">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Appointment">Appointment</span></h3>
<p>On 13 July 2016, two days after becoming Leader of the Conservative Party, May was appointed Prime Minister by <a href="/wiki/Monarchy_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Monarchy of the United Kingdom">Queen</a> <a href="/wiki/Elizabeth_II" title="Elizabeth II">Elizabeth II</a>, becoming only the second female British prime minister after <a href="/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher" title="Margaret Thatcher">Margaret Thatcher</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-166" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-166">&#91;166&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BBC11July_167-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC11July-167">&#91;167&#93;</a></sup> Addressing the world's media outside <a href="/wiki/10_Downing_Street" title="10 Downing Street">10 Downing Street</a>, May said that she was "honoured and humbled" to become prime minister. On becoming prime minister, May became the first woman to have held two of the <a href="/wiki/Great_Offices_of_State" title="Great Offices of State">Great Offices of State</a>.
</p><p>Responding to some calls for an early general election, "sources close to Mrs May" said there was no need for such an election.<sup id="cite_ref-168" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-168">&#91;168&#93;</a></sup> In a speech after her appointment, May emphasised the term "Unionist" in the name of the <a href="/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK)" title="Conservative Party (UK)">Conservative Party</a>, reminding all of "the precious, precious bond between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland."<sup id="cite_ref-169" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-169">&#91;169&#93;</a></sup> By 15 July, May had travelled to <a href="/wiki/Edinburgh" title="Edinburgh">Edinburgh</a> to meet with <a href="/wiki/First_Minister_of_Scotland" title="First Minister of Scotland">First Minister</a> <a href="/wiki/Nicola_Sturgeon" title="Nicola Sturgeon">Nicola Sturgeon</a> to reinforce the bond between Scotland and the rest of the United Kingdom. "I'm coming here to show my commitment to preserving this special union that has endured for centuries," she explained.<sup id="cite_ref-stewart1_170-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-stewart1-170">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Cabinet_changes">Cabinet changes</span></h3>
<p>May's first Cabinet appointment was described by <a href="/wiki/Reuters" title="Reuters">Reuters</a> as "one of the most sweeping government reshuffles for decades", and called "a brutal cull" by <i><a href="/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph" title="The Daily Telegraph">The Daily Telegraph</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-171" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-171">&#91;171&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-masscull_172-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-masscull-172">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup> Nine of Cameron's ministers, including several prominent members, were sacked or resigned from their posts.<sup id="cite_ref-masscull_172-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-masscull-172">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup> The early appointments were interpreted both as an effort to reunite the Conservative Party in the wake of the UK's vote to leave the EU and as "a shift to the right," according to <i><a href="/wiki/The_Guardian" title="The Guardian">The Guardian</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-Center&amp;Right_173-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Center&amp;Right-173">&#91;173&#93;</a></sup> ITV's Political Editor <a href="/wiki/Robert_Peston" title="Robert Peston">Robert Peston</a> commented: "Her rhetoric is more left-wing than Cameron's was, her cabinet is more right-wing than his was."<sup id="cite_ref-174" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-174">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup> Although May had supported remaining in the EU, she appointed several of the most prominent advocates of <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">Brexit</a> to key Cabinet positions responsible for negotiating the <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom_withdrawal_from_the_European_Union" class="mw-redirect" title="United Kingdom withdrawal from the European Union">United Kingdom withdrawal from the European Union</a>, including <a href="/wiki/Boris_Johnson" title="Boris Johnson">Boris Johnson</a> as <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs" class="mw-redirect" title="Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs">Foreign Secretary</a>, <a href="/wiki/David_Davis_(British_politician)" title="David Davis (British politician)">David Davis</a> as <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Exiting_the_European_Union" title="Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union">Brexit Secretary</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Liam_Fox" title="Liam Fox">Liam Fox</a> as <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_International_Trade" title="Secretary of State for International Trade">International Trade Secretary</a>, the latter two being new positions.<sup id="cite_ref-stewart1_170-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-stewart1-170">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-175" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-175">&#91;175&#93;</a></sup> Other key appointees included <a href="/wiki/Amber_Rudd" title="Amber Rudd">Amber Rudd</a> as <a href="/wiki/Home_Secretary" title="Home Secretary">Home Secretary</a> and <a href="/wiki/Philip_Hammond" title="Philip Hammond">Philip Hammond</a> as <a href="/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer" title="Chancellor of the Exchequer">Chancellor of the Exchequer</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-176" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-176">&#91;176&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="First_term_.282016.E2.80.932017.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="First_term_(2016–2017)">First term (2016–2017)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/First_May_ministry" title="First May ministry">First May ministry</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Vladimir_Putin_and_Theresa_May_(2016-09-04)_02.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Vladimir_Putin_and_Theresa_May_%282016-09-04%29_02.jpg/220px-Vladimir_Putin_and_Theresa_May_%282016-09-04%29_02.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="136" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Vladimir_Putin_and_Theresa_May_%282016-09-04%29_02.jpg/330px-Vladimir_Putin_and_Theresa_May_%282016-09-04%29_02.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Vladimir_Putin_and_Theresa_May_%282016-09-04%29_02.jpg/440px-Vladimir_Putin_and_Theresa_May_%282016-09-04%29_02.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1880" data-file-height="1160" /></a><figcaption>May and <a href="/wiki/Vladimir_Putin" title="Vladimir Putin">Vladimir Putin</a> during the <a href="/wiki/2016_G20_Hangzhou_summit" title="2016 G20 Hangzhou summit">G20 summit</a> in <a href="/wiki/Hangzhou" title="Hangzhou">Hangzhou</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/First_May_ministry" title="First May ministry">First May ministry</a> delayed the final approval for the <a href="/wiki/Hinkley_Point_C_nuclear_power_station" title="Hinkley Point C nuclear power station">Hinkley Point C nuclear power station</a> in July 2016, a project which May had objected to when she was Home Secretary.<sup id="cite_ref-177" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-177">&#91;177&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-178">&#91;178&#93;</a></sup> Her <a href="/wiki/Special_advisers_(UK_government)" class="mw-redirect" title="Special advisers (UK government)">political adviser</a> <a href="/wiki/Nick_Timothy" title="Nick Timothy">Nick Timothy</a> wrote an article in 2015 to oppose <a href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</a>'s involvement in sensitive sectors. He said that the government was "selling our <a href="/wiki/National_security" title="National security">national security</a> to China" without <a href="/wiki/Rational" class="mw-redirect" title="Rational">rational</a> concerns and "the Government seems intent on ignoring the evidence and presumably the advice of the security and intelligence agencies".<sup id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-179">&#91;179&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theresa_May_71st_session_of_UNGA.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Theresa_May_71st_session_of_UNGA.jpg/220px-Theresa_May_71st_session_of_UNGA.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Theresa_May_71st_session_of_UNGA.jpg/330px-Theresa_May_71st_session_of_UNGA.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Theresa_May_71st_session_of_UNGA.jpg/440px-Theresa_May_71st_session_of_UNGA.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4393" data-file-height="2929" /></a><figcaption>May addressing the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly" title="United Nations General Assembly">United Nations General Assembly</a> in 2016</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:PM_meeting_with_President_Rouhani_of_Iran_at_UNGA_(29738823751).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/PM_meeting_with_President_Rouhani_of_Iran_at_UNGA_%2829738823751%29.jpg/220px-PM_meeting_with_President_Rouhani_of_Iran_at_UNGA_%2829738823751%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/PM_meeting_with_President_Rouhani_of_Iran_at_UNGA_%2829738823751%29.jpg/330px-PM_meeting_with_President_Rouhani_of_Iran_at_UNGA_%2829738823751%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/PM_meeting_with_President_Rouhani_of_Iran_at_UNGA_%2829738823751%29.jpg/440px-PM_meeting_with_President_Rouhani_of_Iran_at_UNGA_%2829738823751%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3560" data-file-height="2671" /></a><figcaption>Theresa May meets with <a href="/wiki/Hassan_Rouhani" title="Hassan Rouhani">Hassan Rouhani</a> in 2016 in <a href="/wiki/New_York_City" title="New York City">New York City</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>In July 2016, when <a href="/wiki/George_Kerevan" title="George Kerevan">George Kerevan</a> asked her whether she would be prepared to authorise the killing of a hundred thousand innocent persons by a nuclear strike; during the "<a href="/wiki/Trident_nuclear_programme" class="mw-redirect" title="Trident nuclear programme">Trident</a> debate" inside the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="House of Commons of the United Kingdom">House of Commons</a>, May said "Yes. And I have to say to the honourable gentleman: the whole point of a deterrent is that our enemies need to know that we would be prepared to use it. Unlike <a href="/wiki/Political_positions_of_Jeremy_Corbyn#Nuclear_weapons" title="Political positions of Jeremy Corbyn">some suggestions</a> that we could have a nuclear deterrent but not actually be willing to use it, which come from the <a href="/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK)" title="Labour Party (UK)">Labour Party</a> <a href="/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Jeremy_Corbyn" title="Shadow Cabinet of Jeremy Corbyn">frontbench</a>."<sup id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-180">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 20 July, May attended her first <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister%27s_Questions" title="Prime Minister&#39;s Questions">Prime Minister's Questions</a> since taking office, then afterwards made her first <a href="/wiki/List_of_international_prime_ministerial_trips_made_by_Theresa_May" title="List of international prime ministerial trips made by Theresa May">overseas trip as prime minister</a>, visiting Berlin for talks with German Chancellor <a href="/wiki/Angela_Merkel" title="Angela Merkel">Angela Merkel</a>. During the visit, May said that she would not trigger <a href="/wiki/UK_Invocation_of_Article_50" class="mw-redirect" title="UK Invocation of Article 50">Article 50 of the Treaty of Lisbon</a>—the process for withdrawing from the European Union—before 2017, suggesting it would take time for the UK to negotiate a "sensible and orderly departure" from the EU. However, although Merkel said it was right for the UK to "take a moment" before beginning the process, she urged May to provide more clarity on a timetable for negotiations. Shortly before travelling to Berlin, May had also announced that in the wake of the referendum, Britain would relinquish the <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_the_Council_of_the_European_Union" title="Presidency of the Council of the European Union">presidency of the Council of the European Union</a>, which passes between member states every six months on a rotation basis, and that the UK had been scheduled to hold in the second half of 2017.<sup id="cite_ref-181" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-181">&#91;181&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-182">&#91;182&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May supported the <a href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabian-led_intervention_in_Yemen" class="mw-redirect" title="Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen">Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen</a> and defended selling arms to <a href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabia" title="Saudi Arabia">Saudi Arabia</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-183" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-183">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup> which is accused of committing war crimes in Yemen,<sup id="cite_ref-184" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-184">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup> insisting that Britain's close relationship with Saudi Arabia was "helping keep people on the streets of Britain safe".<sup id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-185">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Donald_Trump_and_PM_Theresa_May_Joint_Press_Conference,_January_27,_2017.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/President_Donald_Trump_and_PM_Theresa_May_Joint_Press_Conference%2C_January_27%2C_2017.jpg/220px-President_Donald_Trump_and_PM_Theresa_May_Joint_Press_Conference%2C_January_27%2C_2017.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/President_Donald_Trump_and_PM_Theresa_May_Joint_Press_Conference%2C_January_27%2C_2017.jpg/330px-President_Donald_Trump_and_PM_Theresa_May_Joint_Press_Conference%2C_January_27%2C_2017.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/President_Donald_Trump_and_PM_Theresa_May_Joint_Press_Conference%2C_January_27%2C_2017.jpg/440px-President_Donald_Trump_and_PM_Theresa_May_Joint_Press_Conference%2C_January_27%2C_2017.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1365" /></a><figcaption>May and <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump" title="Donald Trump">Donald Trump</a> in Washington, D.C., January 2017</figcaption></figure>
<p>On 21 January 2017, following the <a href="/wiki/Inauguration_of_Donald_Trump" title="Inauguration of Donald Trump">inauguration of Donald Trump</a> as <a href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">US President</a>, the <a href="/wiki/White_House" title="White House">White House</a> announced that May would meet the President on 27 January, making her the first foreign leader to meet Trump since he took office on 20 January.<sup id="cite_ref-186" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-186">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup> In a joint press conference, May indicated an interest in increased trade between the United States and the United Kingdom. She also affirmed a desire to maintain an American involvement in NATO.<sup id="cite_ref-187" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-187">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup> May was criticised by members of major parties, including her own, for refusing to condemn Trump's <a href="/wiki/Executive_Order_13769" title="Executive Order 13769">Executive Order 13769</a>, as well as for inviting Trump to a state visit with <a href="/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Queen Elizabeth II">Queen Elizabeth II</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-188" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-188">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-bi1_189-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bi1-189">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-190" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-190">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In January 2017, when it came to light that a Trident test had malfunctioned in June 2016, May refused to confirm whether she knew about the incident when she addressed parliament.<sup id="cite_ref-191" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-191">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-192" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-192">&#91;192&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-193" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-193">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:2017_G20_Hamburg_summit_leaders_group_photo.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/2017_G20_Hamburg_summit_leaders_group_photo.jpg/220px-2017_G20_Hamburg_summit_leaders_group_photo.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="136" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/2017_G20_Hamburg_summit_leaders_group_photo.jpg/330px-2017_G20_Hamburg_summit_leaders_group_photo.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/2017_G20_Hamburg_summit_leaders_group_photo.jpg/440px-2017_G20_Hamburg_summit_leaders_group_photo.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1880" data-file-height="1160" /></a><figcaption>May at the <a href="/wiki/2017_G20_Hamburg_summit" title="2017 G20 Hamburg summit">G20 summit</a> in <a href="/wiki/Hamburg" title="Hamburg">Hamburg</a>, 7–8 July 2017</figcaption></figure>
<p>May's Chancellor, <a href="/wiki/Philip_Hammond" title="Philip Hammond">Philip Hammond</a>, continued government policies of freezing benefits in his 2017 budget.<sup id="cite_ref-194" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-194">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="2017_general_election">2017 general election</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2017 United Kingdom general election">2017 United Kingdom general election</a></div>
<p>On 18 April, May announced that she would call a parliamentary vote to hold an <a href="/wiki/Snap_election" title="Snap election">early general election</a> on 8 June, saying that it was the "only way to guarantee certainty and security for years ahead".<sup id="cite_ref-BBC_snap_election_195-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_snap_election-195">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup> May had previously ruled out an early election on five occasions over nine months.<sup id="cite_ref-196" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-196">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup> The election was the first snap election held under the <a href="/wiki/Fixed-term_Parliaments_Act_2011" title="Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011">Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011</a> after MPs gave May the two-thirds <a href="/wiki/Super-majority" class="mw-redirect" title="Super-majority">super-majority</a> required.<sup id="cite_ref-197" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-197">&#91;197&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Unveiling the Conservative manifesto in <a href="/wiki/Halifax,_West_Yorkshire" title="Halifax, West Yorkshire">Halifax</a> on 18 May, May promised a "mainstream government that would deliver for mainstream Britain".<sup id="cite_ref-:13_198-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:13-198">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> It proposed to balance the budget by 2025, raise spending on the NHS by £8bn per annum and on schools by £4bn per annum by 2022, remove the ban on new <a href="/wiki/Grammar_school" title="Grammar school">grammar schools</a>, <a href="/wiki/Means-tested_benefit" class="mw-redirect" title="Means-tested benefit">means-test</a> the <a href="/wiki/Winter_Fuel_Payment" title="Winter Fuel Payment">winter fuel allowance</a>, replace the <a href="/wiki/State_Pension_(United_Kingdom)" title="State Pension (United Kingdom)">state pension</a> "triple lock" with a "double lock" and require executive pay to be approved by a vote of shareholders.<sup id="cite_ref-:13_198-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:13-198">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> It also contained May's previously-announced flagship energy reform of a <a href="/wiki/Energy_policy_of_the_United_Kingdom#2018_to_present:_Default_tariff_energy_price_cap" title="Energy policy of the United Kingdom">cap on gas and electricity bills for households</a> on standard variable tariffs.<sup id="cite_ref-199" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-199">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup> It dropped the 2015 pledge to not raise income tax or national insurance contributions but maintained a commitment to freeze <a href="/wiki/Value-added_tax" title="Value-added tax">VAT</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:13_198-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:13-198">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> New <a href="/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund" title="Sovereign wealth fund">sovereign wealth funds</a> for infrastructure, rules to prevent foreign takeovers of "critical national infrastructure" and <a href="/wiki/Institute_of_technology" title="Institute of technology">institutes of technology</a> were also proposed.<sup id="cite_ref-200" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-200">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup> The manifesto was noted for its intervention in industry, lack of tax cuts and increased spending commitments on public services.<sup id="cite_ref-201" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-201">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup> On Brexit it committed to leaving the single market and <a href="/wiki/European_Union_Customs_Union" title="European Union Customs Union">customs union</a> while seeking a "deep and special partnership" and promised a vote in parliament on the final agreement.<sup id="cite_ref-:14_202-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:14-202">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theresa_May_and_FM_Arlene_Foster.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Theresa_May_and_FM_Arlene_Foster.jpg/150px-Theresa_May_and_FM_Arlene_Foster.jpg" decoding="async" width="150" height="178" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Theresa_May_and_FM_Arlene_Foster.jpg/226px-Theresa_May_and_FM_Arlene_Foster.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Theresa_May_and_FM_Arlene_Foster.jpg/301px-Theresa_May_and_FM_Arlene_Foster.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1580" data-file-height="1870" /></a><figcaption>May with <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Unionist_Party" title="Democratic Unionist Party">Democratic Unionist Party</a> (DUP) leader <a href="/wiki/Arlene_Foster" title="Arlene Foster">Arlene Foster</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The manifesto also proposed reforms to <a href="/wiki/Social_care_in_England" title="Social care in England">social care in England</a> that would raise the threshold for free care from £23,250 to £100,000 while including property in the means test and permitting deferred payment after death.<sup id="cite_ref-:13_198-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:13-198">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> After attracting substantial media attention, four days after the manifesto launch May stated that the proposed social care reforms would now include an "absolute limit" on costs in contrast to the rejection of a cap in the manifesto.<sup id="cite_ref-:16_203-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:16-203">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup> She criticised the "fake" portrayal of the policy in recent days by Labour and other critics who had termed it a "dementia tax".<sup id="cite_ref-:16_203-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:16-203">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/London_Evening_Standard" class="mw-redirect" title="London Evening Standard"><i>Evening Standard</i></a> editor <a href="/wiki/George_Osborne" title="George Osborne">George Osborne</a> called the policy change a "U-turn".<sup id="cite_ref-204" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-204">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup> <i>The Financial Times</i> contrasted her "<a href="/wiki/Strong_and_Stable" class="mw-redirect" title="Strong and Stable">Strong and Stable</a>" leadership slogan with her own record of nine rapid U-turns claiming she was "making a habit of retreating from policies."<sup id="cite_ref-Financial_Times_u_turn_205-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Financial_Times_u_turn-205">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The general election in June resulted in a hung parliament, prompting her to broker a <a href="/wiki/Con%E2%80%93DUP_pact" class="mw-redirect" title="Con–DUP pact">deal</a> with <a href="/wiki/Northern_Ireland" title="Northern Ireland">Northern Ireland</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Unionist_Party" title="Democratic Unionist Party">Democratic Unionist Party</a> (DUP), involving £1 billion of additional public funding for Northern Ireland.<sup id="cite_ref-206" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-206">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-207">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Second_term_.282017.E2.80.932019.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Second_term_(2017–2019)">Second term (2017–2019)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Second_May_ministry" title="Second May ministry">Second May ministry</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Macri_y_May_en_el_G20.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Macri_y_May_en_el_G20.jpg/220px-Macri_y_May_en_el_G20.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="156" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Macri_y_May_en_el_G20.jpg/330px-Macri_y_May_en_el_G20.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Macri_y_May_en_el_G20.jpg/440px-Macri_y_May_en_el_G20.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1920" data-file-height="1364" /></a><figcaption>May with the <a href="/wiki/President_of_Argentina" title="President of Argentina">President of Argentina</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mauricio_Macri" title="Mauricio Macri">Mauricio Macri</a> during the <a href="/wiki/2018_G20_Buenos_Aires_summit" title="2018 G20 Buenos Aires summit">2018 G20 Buenos Aires summit</a>. May is the first British prime minister to visit <a href="/wiki/Buenos_Aires" title="Buenos Aires">Buenos Aires</a> after the <a href="/wiki/Falklands_War" title="Falklands War">Falklands War</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-208" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-208">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>Less than two weeks after the 2017 State Opening of Parliament, May ordered a full <a href="/wiki/Public_inquiry" title="Public inquiry">public inquiry</a> into the <a href="/wiki/Contaminated_blood_scandal_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Contaminated blood scandal in the United Kingdom">contaminated blood scandal</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-209" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-209">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup> For this she was widely praised as successive governments going back to the 1980s had refused such an inquiry, some though speculated that May had simply been forced to announce the inquiry after a group legal action and news of fresh evidence were brought by Jason Evans.<sup id="cite_ref-210" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-210">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-211" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-211">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup> Additionally, Andy Burnham had threatened to take evidence to the police if an inquiry were not announced.<sup id="cite_ref-212" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-212">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup> With over 1,000 core participants, the <a href="/wiki/Infected_Blood_Inquiry" class="mw-redirect" title="Infected Blood Inquiry">Infected Blood Inquiry</a> is the biggest public inquiry ever held in the UK.<sup id="cite_ref-213" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-213">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Myanmar">Myanmar</span></h4>
<p>In November 2017, May said the <a href="/wiki/Rohingya_persecution_in_Myanmar_(2016%E2%80%93present)" class="mw-redirect" title="Rohingya persecution in Myanmar (2016–present)">actions</a> of <a href="/wiki/Myanmar_Army" title="Myanmar Army">Myanmar Army</a> and police against the <a href="/wiki/Rohingya_people" title="Rohingya people">Rohingya Muslim</a> minority in <a href="/wiki/Myanmar" title="Myanmar">Myanmar</a> "looks like ethnic cleansing".<sup id="cite_ref-skynews_214-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-skynews-214">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup> According to May, "it is something for which the Burmese authorities – and especially the military – must take full responsibility."<sup id="cite_ref-skynews_214-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-skynews-214">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup> From the 2017 general election to December 2017, May suffered no defeats in whipped votes in the House of Commons.<sup id="cite_ref-215" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-215">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup> On 13 December 2017, May lost a vote on the <a href="/wiki/EU_Withdrawal_Bill" class="mw-redirect" title="EU Withdrawal Bill">EU Withdrawal Bill</a> by 309 votes to 305, due to 11 Conservatives voting against the government, including <a href="/wiki/Stephen_Hammond" title="Stephen Hammond">Stephen Hammond</a> who was then vice-chairman of the Conservative Party.<sup id="cite_ref-216" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-216">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-217" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-217">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Russia">Russia</span></h4>

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theresa_May_and_Vladimir_Putin_(2019-06-29)_02.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Theresa_May_and_Vladimir_Putin_%282019-06-29%29_02.jpg/220px-Theresa_May_and_Vladimir_Putin_%282019-06-29%29_02.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="136" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Theresa_May_and_Vladimir_Putin_%282019-06-29%29_02.jpg/330px-Theresa_May_and_Vladimir_Putin_%282019-06-29%29_02.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Theresa_May_and_Vladimir_Putin_%282019-06-29%29_02.jpg/440px-Theresa_May_and_Vladimir_Putin_%282019-06-29%29_02.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1880" data-file-height="1160" /></a><figcaption>May with Russian President <a href="/wiki/Vladimir_Putin" title="Vladimir Putin">Vladimir Putin</a> in <a href="/wiki/Osaka" title="Osaka">Osaka</a>, 2019</figcaption></figure>
<p>May accused <a href="/wiki/Russia" title="Russia">Russia</a> of "threatening the international order", "seeking to weaponise information" and "deploying its state-run media organisations to plant fake stories".<sup id="cite_ref-indy_218-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-indy-218">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup> She further suggested the country had been meddling in the <a href="/wiki/2017_German_federal_election" title="2017 German federal election">2017 German federal election</a><sup id="cite_ref-indy_218-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-indy-218">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup> in contradiction of German government officials and security experts, who had dismissed the possibility.<sup id="cite_ref-219" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-219">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May's government accused Russia for orchestrating the <a href="/wiki/Poisoning_of_Sergei_and_Yulia_Skripal" title="Poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal">poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal</a>. The UK's official assessment of this incident was supported by 28 other countries, who expelled an unprecedented total of 153 Russian diplomats.
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="China">China</span></h4>
<p>May promised to confront <a href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</a> on human rights but was praised in <a href="/wiki/Communist_Party_of_China" class="mw-redirect" title="Communist Party of China">Communist Party</a>-controlled <a href="/wiki/Media_of_China" class="mw-redirect" title="Media of China">media</a> for "sidestepping" <a href="/wiki/Human_rights_in_China" title="Human rights in China">human rights in China</a> during her first official visit to the country.<sup id="cite_ref-week_220-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-week-220">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup> The <i><a href="/wiki/Global_Times" title="Global Times">Global Times</a></i> said: "For the Prime Minister, the losses outweigh the gains if she appeases the British media at the cost of the visit's friendly atmosphere."<sup id="cite_ref-week_220-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-week-220">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Assassination_plot">Assassination plot</span></h4>
<p>In 2017, <a href="/wiki/Islamic_State" title="Islamic State">Islamic State</a> terrorist <a href="/wiki/Naa%27imur_Zakariyah_Rahman" title="Naa&#39;imur Zakariyah Rahman">Naa'imur Zakariyah Rahman</a> was foiled in a plot to assassinate May at <a href="/wiki/Downing_Street" title="Downing Street">Downing Street</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-221" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-221">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Turkey">Turkey</span></h4>
<p>In May 2018, during a three-day state visit to the UK by Turkish president <a href="/wiki/Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan" title="Recep Tayyip Erdoğan">Recep Tayyip Erdoğan</a>, May declared that Britain is a "true friend" of <a href="/wiki/Turkey" title="Turkey">Turkey</a>, but she added that "It is important that in defense of democracy, which has been facing extraordinary pressures from the <a href="/wiki/2016_Turkish_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt" class="mw-redirect" title="2016 Turkish coup d&#39;état attempt">failed coup</a>, instability across the border from Syria and from <a href="/wiki/Kurdish%E2%80%93Turkish_conflict_(1978%E2%80%93present)" title="Kurdish–Turkish conflict (1978–present)">Kurdish terrorism</a>, Turkey does not lose sight of the values it is seeking to defend."<sup id="cite_ref-222" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-222">&#91;222&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-223" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-223">&#91;223&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Saudi_Arabia_massacres_civilians_in_Yemen_with_U.K._assistance.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Saudi_Arabia_massacres_civilians_in_Yemen_with_U.K._assistance.jpg/220px-Saudi_Arabia_massacres_civilians_in_Yemen_with_U.K._assistance.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="142" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Saudi_Arabia_massacres_civilians_in_Yemen_with_U.K._assistance.jpg/330px-Saudi_Arabia_massacres_civilians_in_Yemen_with_U.K._assistance.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Saudi_Arabia_massacres_civilians_in_Yemen_with_U.K._assistance.jpg/440px-Saudi_Arabia_massacres_civilians_in_Yemen_with_U.K._assistance.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3727" data-file-height="2402" /></a><figcaption>Theresa May came under criticism for providing support to the <a href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabian-led_intervention_in_Yemen" class="mw-redirect" title="Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen">Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-224" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-224">&#91;224&#93;</a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Contempt_of_Parliament">Contempt of Parliament</span></h4>
<p>On 4 December 2018, on a motion passed by MPs by 311 to 293 votes,<sup id="cite_ref-225" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-225">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Second_May_ministry" title="Second May ministry">May Government</a> was found in <a href="/wiki/Contempt_of_Parliament" title="Contempt of Parliament">contempt of Parliament</a>; the first <a href="/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Government of the United Kingdom">government</a> to be found in contempt in history.<sup id="cite_ref-Please_back_my_deal_Sky_News_226-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Please_back_my_deal_Sky_News-226">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup> The vote was triggered by the government failing to lay before Parliament any legal advice on the proposed withdrawal agreement on the terms of the <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">UK's departure from the European Union</a>, after a <a href="/wiki/Humble_address" title="Humble address">humble address</a> for a return was unanimously agreed to by the House of Commons on 13 November 2018. The government then agreed to publish the full legal advice<sup id="cite_ref-Please_back_my_deal_Sky_News_226-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Please_back_my_deal_Sky_News-226">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup> for <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">Brexit</a> that was given to the <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Prime Minister of the United Kingdom">Prime Minister</a> by the <a href="/wiki/Attorney_General_for_England_and_Wales" title="Attorney General for England and Wales">Attorney General</a> during negotiations with the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a>.
</p>
<h4><span id="Vote_of_confidence_.28Conservative_Party.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Vote_of_confidence_(Conservative_Party)"><span class="anchor" id="Vote_of_confidence"></span>Vote of confidence (Conservative Party)</span></h4>
<p>On 12 December 2018, May faced a vote of confidence in her leadership of the Conservative Party over opposition to her <a href="/wiki/Withdrawal_Agreement" class="mw-redirect" title="Withdrawal Agreement">negotiated Brexit deal</a>, after the number of Conservative MPs exceeded the 48 no-confidence letter threshold that the <a href="/wiki/1922_Committee" title="1922 Committee">1922 Committee Chairman</a>, Sir <a href="/wiki/Graham_Brady" title="Graham Brady">Graham Brady</a> required for the vote of confidence to be held.<sup id="cite_ref-227" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-227">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup> May won the vote with 200 Conservative MPs voting for her, compared to 117 voting against.<sup id="cite_ref-228" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-228">&#91;228&#93;</a></sup> As part of her speech to the <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_Conservative_Party" class="mw-redirect" title="Parliamentary Conservative Party">Parliamentary Conservative Party</a> before the confidence vote was opened, it was reported that May conceded that she would step down as prime minister after delivering <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">Brexit</a> and would not lead the Conservative Party into the next General Election in exchange for Conservative MPs voting to have confidence in her leadership so that she would be able to keep the party, Parliament and the UK stable during the final stages of Brexit. May later confirmed this to <a href="/wiki/BBC_News" title="BBC News">BBC News</a> <a href="/wiki/Political_editor" title="Political editor">Political editor</a>, <a href="/wiki/Laura_Kuenssberg" title="Laura Kuenssberg">Laura Kuenssberg</a> after meeting EU leaders, including <a href="/wiki/Jean-Claude_Juncker" title="Jean-Claude Juncker">Jean-Claude Juncker</a> in <a href="/wiki/Brussels" title="Brussels">Brussels</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-auto_229-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto-229">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id="Vote_of_no_confidence_.28House_of_Commons.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Vote_of_no_confidence_(House_of_Commons)">Vote of no confidence (House of Commons)</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/2019_vote_of_confidence_in_the_May_ministry" title="2019 vote of confidence in the May ministry">2019 vote of confidence in the May ministry</a></div>
<p>On 17 December 2018 in the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="House of Commons of the United Kingdom">House of Commons</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(United_Kingdom)" title="Leader of the Opposition (United Kingdom)">Leader of the Opposition</a> and <a href="/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK)" title="Leader of the Labour Party (UK)">Labour Party Leader</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn" title="Jeremy Corbyn">Jeremy Corbyn</a>, tabled a <a href="/wiki/Motion_of_no_confidence" title="Motion of no confidence">motion of no confidence</a> in May's <a href="/wiki/Premiership_of_Theresa_May" title="Premiership of Theresa May">premiership</a>, citing May's refusal to set the date for the <a href="/wiki/Meaningful_vote" class="mw-redirect" title="Meaningful vote">meaningful vote</a> on her Brexit deal before Christmas, and instead pushing it back to mid-January.<sup id="cite_ref-230" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-230">&#91;230&#93;</a></sup> The following day the <a href="/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Government of the United Kingdom">government</a> refused to allow time for the motion to be debated. <a href="/wiki/John_Bercow" title="John Bercow">John Bercow</a>, <a href="/wiki/Speaker_of_the_House_of_Commons_(United_Kingdom)" title="Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)">Speaker of the House of Commons</a>, confirmed that they were under no obligation to do so.<sup id="cite_ref-231" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-231">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup> Following the defeat of May's Brexit deal on 15 January 2019, Corbyn tabled a <a href="/wiki/2019_motion_of_no_confidence_in_the_May_ministry" class="mw-redirect" title="2019 motion of no confidence in the May ministry">motion of no confidence</a> in the Government, to be voted on by parliament the following evening.<sup id="cite_ref-232" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-232">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-233" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-233">&#91;233&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-234" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-234">&#91;234&#93;</a></sup> The motion was defeated by 325 votes to 306; a majority of 19.
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Brexit_deal_defeats">Brexit deal defeats</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_votes_on_Brexit" title="Parliamentary votes on Brexit">Parliamentary votes on Brexit</a></div>
<p>On 15 January 2019, May's government was defeated in the House of Commons by a margin of 230 votes (202 in favour and 432 opposed) in a vote on her deal to leave the European Union ("first meaningful vote"). It was the largest majority against a United Kingdom government in history.<sup id="cite_ref-235" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-235">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 12 March, May was again defeated in the Commons by 149 votes (242 in favour and 391 against) on her latest deal after she secured last-minute concessions from the EU ("second meaningful vote").<sup id="cite_ref-236" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-236">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 29 March, May was again defeated by 58 votes in the Commons (286 in favour and 344 against) on the withdrawal deal but not the political declaration ("third meaningful vote").<sup id="cite_ref-237" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-237">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Resignation">Resignation</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/2019_Conservative_Party_(UK)_leadership_election" class="mw-redirect" title="2019 Conservative Party (UK) leadership election">2019 Conservative Party (UK) leadership election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Theresa_May_declares_resignation.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Theresa_May_declares_resignation.jpg/220px-Theresa_May_declares_resignation.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Theresa_May_declares_resignation.jpg/330px-Theresa_May_declares_resignation.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Theresa_May_declares_resignation.jpg/440px-Theresa_May_declares_resignation.jpg 2x" data-file-width="960" data-file-height="640" /></a><figcaption>May announces her resignation outside 10 Downing Street on 24 May 2019</figcaption></figure>
<p>On 27 March 2019 at a meeting of the <a href="/wiki/1922_Committee" title="1922 Committee">1922 Committee</a>, May confirmed that she will "not lead the UK in the next stage of <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">Brexit</a> negotiations", meaning she was expected to resign after the third meaningful vote, if it had passed successfully.<sup id="cite_ref-autogenerated1_238-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-autogenerated1-238">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup> However, no date was stated, and her reported wording was ambiguous and thus carried no binding force.<sup id="cite_ref-autogenerated1_238-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-autogenerated1-238">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup> On 29 March, the third meaningful vote was defeated, and while May did not state anything in regards to standing down, Corbyn stated that if May could not find an alternative to her deal "she must go, not at an indeterminate date in the future but now."<sup id="cite_ref-239" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-239">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 22 April it was announced that the leaders of 70 <a href="/wiki/Conservative_Association" title="Conservative Association">Conservative Associations</a> had signed a petition calling for a vote of no confidence. Under party rules an Extraordinary General Meeting must be convened if one is demanded by 65 associations. The non-binding vote, to be determined by 800 of the party's senior officials, would be the first time such an instance has occurred.<sup id="cite_ref-240" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-240">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup> On 24 April, the party's <a href="/wiki/1922_Committee" title="1922 Committee">1922 Committee</a> ruled out changing the leadership challenge rules, but its chair, <a href="/wiki/Graham_Brady" title="Graham Brady">Graham Brady</a>, asked for clarity on when May would step down from office.<sup id="cite_ref-241" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-241">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 24 May she confirmed that she would resign as <a href="/wiki/Leader_of_the_Conservative_Party_(UK)" title="Leader of the Conservative Party (UK)">Conservative Party leader</a> on 7 June,<sup id="cite_ref-BBC_resignation_24_May_242-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_resignation_24_May-242">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup> stating, "it is now clear to me that it is in the best interests of the country for a new prime minister to lead <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">that effort</a>."<sup id="cite_ref-243" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-243">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup> She continued to serve as prime minister until she tendered her resignation to <a href="/wiki/Elizabeth_II" title="Elizabeth II">the Queen</a> on 24 July. This coincided with the arrival of <a href="/wiki/Boris_Johnson" title="Boris Johnson">Boris Johnson</a> as prime minister, who was <a href="/wiki/2019_Conservative_Party_(UK)_leadership_election" class="mw-redirect" title="2019 Conservative Party (UK) leadership election">elected</a> by the Conservative Party membership.<sup id="cite_ref-Tory_244-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Tory-244">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup> By constitutional convention May did not step down until she assured the Queen that Johnson would be able to command the confidence of the House of Commons.<sup id="cite_ref-245" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-245">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In one of May's last <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister%27s_Questions" title="Prime Minister&#39;s Questions">Prime Minister's Questions</a>, <a href="/wiki/Barry_Sheerman" title="Barry Sheerman">Barry Sheerman</a>, the Labour MP for <a href="/wiki/Huddersfield_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Huddersfield (UK Parliament constituency)">Huddersfield</a>, urged May not to "cut and run" and instead reconsider her resignation. May responded by saying she would return to the role of a backbench MP after leaving office.<sup id="cite_ref-246" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-246">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 24 July 2019, May ended her consecutive service at the frontbench since 1998 when she had been appointed Shadow Spokesman for Schools, Disabled People and Women.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Ministerial_resignations">Ministerial resignations</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/List_of_departures_from_the_second_May_ministry" title="List of departures from the second May ministry">List of departures from the second May ministry</a></div>
<p>May's premiership had 51 resignations with 33 relating to Brexit. These included 12 departures from the Cabinet. The pace and number of resignations have been described as 'unprecedented' by the <a href="/wiki/Institute_for_Government" title="Institute for Government">Institute for Government</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-247" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-247">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup> with resignations impacting the functioning of the government.<sup id="cite_ref-248" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-248">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup> In less than three years, May received more resignations than <a href="/wiki/Premiership_of_Margaret_Thatcher" title="Premiership of Margaret Thatcher">Thatcher</a> (11 years) or <a href="/wiki/Premiership_of_Tony_Blair" title="Premiership of Tony Blair">Blair</a> (10 years). The <a href="/wiki/Chief_Whip" title="Chief Whip">Chief Whip</a> <a href="/wiki/Julian_Smith_(politician)" title="Julian Smith (politician)">Julian Smith</a> described May's Cabinet as exhibiting the 'worst cabinet ill-discipline in history'.<sup id="cite_ref-249" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-249">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Public_opinion">Public opinion</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Leadership_approval_opinion_polling_for_the_2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#Preferred_Prime_Minister_polling" title="Leadership approval opinion polling for the 2019 United Kingdom general election">Leadership approval opinion polling for the 2019 United Kingdom general election §&#160;Preferred Prime Minister polling</a></div>
<p>May had a high approval rating during her first week as prime minister. The results of an Ipsos MORI survey released in July 2016 indicated that 55% of those surveyed believed that May was a suitable PM while only 23% believed that the Labour Leader Jeremy Corbyn would make a good prime minister.<sup id="cite_ref-250" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-250">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>A <i>ComRes</i> poll taken in September 2016 after her election suggested May was seen as substantially more "in touch with ordinary British people" than her predecessor David Cameron and a majority of voters saw her as "the right person to unite the country".<sup id="cite_ref-251" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-251">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>At the beginning of 2017, nearly six months after becoming prime minister, a <a href="/wiki/ComRes" class="mw-redirect" title="ComRes">ComRes</a> found May was the most popular UK politician with a net rating of +9 which was described as the longest honeymoon period enjoyed by any sitting Conservative prime minister since the end of the Second World War.<sup id="cite_ref-252" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-252">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-253" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-253">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Conservative Party had a 21-point lead over Labour in a poll released the day before May announced a snap election<sup id="cite_ref-254" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-254">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup> but this lead narrowed substantially.<sup id="cite_ref-255" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-255">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup> In mid-June, following the election, a YouGov poll showed that May's popularity had dropped to a rating of −34.<sup id="cite_ref-256" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-256">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup> In April 2018, May had a higher approval rating than Corbyn for the first time since the general election, leading him by −13 to −23.<sup id="cite_ref-257" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-257">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Plans to reform <a href="/wiki/Social_care_in_England" title="Social care in England">social care</a> came to dominate the Conservative election campaign during the 2017 Snap Election, with some arguing it ultimately cost May her majority.<sup id="cite_ref-258" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-258">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-259" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-259">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup> May's promised <a href="/wiki/Green_paper#United_Kingdom" title="Green paper">green paper</a> on the future of adult social care was plagued by frequent delays, ultimately never materialising during her premiership.<sup id="cite_ref-260" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-260">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup> A December 2019 poll by <a href="/wiki/Learning_disabilities" class="mw-redirect" title="Learning disabilities">learning disabilities</a> charity Hft found that 59% of social care providers in England believed that the situation in social care worsened under May's premiership, compared to just 3% who said it was slightly better.<sup id="cite_ref-261" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-261">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
