<ul><li><span class="noviewer" typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/DodgerBlue_flag_waving.svg/15px-DodgerBlue_flag_waving.svg.png" decoding="async" width="15" height="16" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/DodgerBlue_flag_waving.svg/22px-DodgerBlue_flag_waving.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/DodgerBlue_flag_waving.svg/30px-DodgerBlue_flag_waving.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="249" data-file-height="268" /></span></span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Portal:Conservatism" title="Portal:Conservatism">Conservatism&#32;portal</a></li>
<li><span class="mw-image-border noviewer" typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:A_coloured_voting_box.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="icon" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/01/A_coloured_voting_box.svg/16px-A_coloured_voting_box.svg.png" decoding="async" width="16" height="16" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/01/A_coloured_voting_box.svg/24px-A_coloured_voting_box.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/01/A_coloured_voting_box.svg/32px-A_coloured_voting_box.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="160" data-file-height="160" /></a></span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Portal:Politics" title="Portal:Politics">Politics&#32;portal</a></li>
<li><span class="mw-image-border noviewer" typeof="mw:File"><span><img alt="flag" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/Flag_of_the_United_Kingdom.svg/16px-Flag_of_the_United_Kingdom.svg.png" decoding="async" width="16" height="8" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/Flag_of_the_United_Kingdom.svg/24px-Flag_of_the_United_Kingdom.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/Flag_of_the_United_Kingdom.svg/32px-Flag_of_the_United_Kingdom.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="600" /></span></span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Portal:United_Kingdom" title="Portal:United Kingdom">United Kingdom&#32;portal</a></li></ul></td></tr><tr><td class="sidebar-navbar"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1129693374"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1063604349"><div class="navbar plainlinks hlist navbar-mini"><ul><li class="nv-view"><a href="/wiki/Template:One-nation_conservatism" title="Template:One-nation conservatism"><abbr title="View this template">v</abbr></a></li><li class="nv-talk"><a href="/wiki/Template_talk:One-nation_conservatism" title="Template talk:One-nation conservatism"><abbr title="Discuss this template">t</abbr></a></li><li class="nv-edit"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Template:One-nation_conservatism&amp;action=edit"><abbr title="Edit this template">e</abbr></a></li></ul></div></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>May has identified herself with the <a href="/wiki/One_nation_conservatism" class="mw-redirect" title="One nation conservatism">one-nation conservative</a> position within her party.<sup id="cite_ref-262" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-262">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Since coming into prominence as a front-bench politician, May's public image has divided media opinion, especially from some in the traditionalist right-wing press.<sup id="cite_ref-263" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-263">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup> Commenting on May's debut as Home Secretary, Anne Perkins of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Guardian" title="The Guardian">The Guardian</a></i> observed that "she'll be nobody's stooge",<sup id="cite_ref-264" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-264">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup> while <a href="/wiki/Cristina_Odone" title="Cristina Odone">Cristina Odone</a> of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph" title="The Daily Telegraph">The Daily Telegraph</a></i> predicted her to be "the rising star" of the Coalition Government.<sup id="cite_ref-265" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-265">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Allegra_Stratton" title="Allegra Stratton">Allegra Stratton</a>, then with <i>The Guardian</i>, praised May as showing managerial acumen.<sup id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-266">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Describing her as a <a href="/wiki/Liberal_Conservative" class="mw-redirect" title="Liberal Conservative">liberal Conservative</a>, the <i><a href="/wiki/Financial_Times" title="Financial Times">Financial Times</a></i> characterised May as a "non-ideological politician with a ruthless streak who gets on with the job", in doing so comparing her to German Chancellor <a href="/wiki/Angela_Merkel" title="Angela Merkel">Angela Merkel</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Warrell_267-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Warrell-267">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> Conversely, in <i><a href="/wiki/The_Independent" title="The Independent">The Independent</a></i>, Rebecca Glover of the Policy Innovation Research Unit contrasted May to <a href="/wiki/Boris_Johnson" title="Boris Johnson">Boris Johnson</a>, claiming that she was "staunchly more conservative, more anti-immigration, and more isolationist" than he was.<sup id="cite_ref-268" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-268">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During her leadership campaign, May said that "We need an economy that works for everyone", pledging to crack down on executive pay by making shareholders' votes binding rather than advisory and to put workers onto company boards<sup id="cite_ref-269" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-269">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup> (although she later claimed that the last pledge was not to be mandatory<sup id="cite_ref-270" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-270">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup>), policies that <i>The Guardian</i> describes as going further than the <a href="/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK)" title="Labour Party (UK)">Labour Party's</a> <a href="/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2015 United Kingdom general election">2015 general election</a> manifesto.<sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:First_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_at_Bute_House_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/First_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_at_Bute_House_%28cropped%29.jpg/220px-First_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_at_Bute_House_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="243" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/First_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_at_Bute_House_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-First_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_at_Bute_House_%28cropped%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a5/First_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_at_Bute_House_%28cropped%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="400" data-file-height="441" /></a><figcaption>May's first visit since becoming prime minister with <a href="/wiki/First_Minister_of_Scotland" title="First Minister of Scotland">First Minister of Scotland</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nicola_Sturgeon" title="Nicola Sturgeon">Nicola Sturgeon</a>, at <a href="/wiki/Bute_House" title="Bute House">Bute House</a>, <a href="/wiki/Edinburgh" title="Edinburgh">Edinburgh</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>After she became prime minister, May's first speech espoused the left, with a promise to combat the "burning injustice" in British society and to create a union "between all of our citizens" and promising to be an advocate for the "ordinary working-class family" and not for the affluent in the UK. "The government I lead will be driven not by the interests of the privileged few but by yours. We will do everything we can to give you more control over your lives ... When we take the big calls, we'll think not of the powerful, but you. When we pass new laws we'll listen not to the mighty, but to you. When it comes to taxes we'll prioritise not the wealthy but you."<sup id="cite_ref-272" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-272">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May has described herself as a personal supporter of fox hunting with hounds, saying that foxes' numbers had to be controlled and that hunting them with dogs was the most humane way to do it. The Conservative manifesto for the 2017 election included a pledge to hold a parliamentary vote to repeal the <a href="/wiki/Hunting_Act_2004" title="Hunting Act 2004">Hunting Act 2004</a>, which prohibits a range of hunting activities.<sup id="cite_ref-273" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-273">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the Conservatives' manifesto for the 2017 election was released, some people, including <a href="/wiki/Fraser_Nelson" title="Fraser Nelson">Fraser Nelson</a> of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Spectator" title="The Spectator">The Spectator</a></i>,<sup id="cite_ref-Nelson_2017_274-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Nelson_2017-274">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup> called her a "<a href="/wiki/Red_Tory" title="Red Tory">red Tory</a>", saying that she had moved her party to the <a href="/wiki/Left-wing_politics" title="Left-wing politics">left</a> in politics. <i><a href="/wiki/Politico" title="Politico">Politico</a></i> called her policies "Mayism", saying that Mayism was "a working-class conservatism openly critical of the "cult of individualism" and globalization".<sup id="cite_ref-Wright_2017_275-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Wright_2017-275">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Cooper_2017_276-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Cooper_2017-276">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May praised the former Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Winston_Churchill" title="Winston Churchill">Winston Churchill</a> and has a portrait of Churchill on the wall of her study. May's spokesman said: "The prime minister has quoted and referenced Sir Winston Churchill on many occasion and acknowledged him as one of the great prime ministers of the 20th century."<sup id="cite_ref-277" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-277">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May welcomed the arrest of WikiLeaks founder <a href="/wiki/Julian_Assange" title="Julian Assange">Julian Assange</a>, saying that "no one is above the law."<sup id="cite_ref-278" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-278">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup> Assange had fled to the Ecuadorian embassy in London in 2012 after being accused of sexual assault in Sweden. He is also wanted by the US for "conspiracy to commit computer intrusion" relating to the Wikileaks release of classified material in 2010, including footage of US soldiers killing civilians in Iraq.<sup id="cite_ref-279" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-279">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-280" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-280">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Foreign_policy">Foreign policy</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:May_meets_with_Aung_San_Suu_Kyi_in_2016.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/May_meets_with_Aung_San_Suu_Kyi_in_2016.jpg/220px-May_meets_with_Aung_San_Suu_Kyi_in_2016.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/May_meets_with_Aung_San_Suu_Kyi_in_2016.jpg/330px-May_meets_with_Aung_San_Suu_Kyi_in_2016.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/May_meets_with_Aung_San_Suu_Kyi_in_2016.jpg/440px-May_meets_with_Aung_San_Suu_Kyi_in_2016.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3433" data-file-height="2289" /></a><figcaption>May meeting with State Counsellor of <a href="/wiki/Myanmar" title="Myanmar">Myanmar</a> and Nobel Peace Prize laureate <a href="/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi" title="Aung San Suu Kyi">Aung San Suu Kyi</a> in September 2016</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Trump_and_First_Lady_Melania_Trump%27s_Trip_to_the_United_Kingdom_(48007684456).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/President_Trump_and_First_Lady_Melania_Trump%27s_Trip_to_the_United_Kingdom_%2848007684456%29.jpg/220px-President_Trump_and_First_Lady_Melania_Trump%27s_Trip_to_the_United_Kingdom_%2848007684456%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="107" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/President_Trump_and_First_Lady_Melania_Trump%27s_Trip_to_the_United_Kingdom_%2848007684456%29.jpg/330px-President_Trump_and_First_Lady_Melania_Trump%27s_Trip_to_the_United_Kingdom_%2848007684456%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/President_Trump_and_First_Lady_Melania_Trump%27s_Trip_to_the_United_Kingdom_%2848007684456%29.jpg/440px-President_Trump_and_First_Lady_Melania_Trump%27s_Trip_to_the_United_Kingdom_%2848007684456%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1128" data-file-height="551" /></a><figcaption>May with <a href="/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Queen Elizabeth II">Queen Elizabeth II</a> and other world leaders to mark the 75th anniversary of <a href="/wiki/D-Day" class="mw-redirect" title="D-Day">D-Day</a> on 5 June 2019</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 2003, May <a href="/wiki/British_Parliamentary_approval_for_the_invasion_of_Iraq" class="mw-redirect" title="British Parliamentary approval for the invasion of Iraq">voted to approve the invasion of Iraq</a> and in 2013 voted in favour of <a href="/wiki/Operation_Shader#Airstrikes_in_Syria" title="Operation Shader">British military intervention</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Syrian_civil_war" title="Syrian civil war">Syrian civil war</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-281" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-281">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/First_May_ministry" title="First May ministry">May Ministry</a> delayed the final approval for the <a href="/wiki/Hinkley_Point_C_nuclear_power_station" title="Hinkley Point C nuclear power station">Hinkley Point C nuclear power station</a> in July 2016, a project which May had objected to when she was Home Secretary.<sup id="cite_ref-282" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-282">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-283" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-283">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup> Her <a href="/wiki/Special_advisers_(UK_government)" class="mw-redirect" title="Special advisers (UK government)">political adviser</a> <a href="/wiki/Nick_Timothy" title="Nick Timothy">Nick Timothy</a> wrote an article in 2015 to oppose People's Republic of China's involvement in sensitive sectors. He said that the government was "selling our <a href="/wiki/National_security" title="National security">national security</a> to China" without <a href="/wiki/Rational" class="mw-redirect" title="Rational">rational</a> concerns and "the Government seems intent on ignoring the evidence and presumably the advice of the security and intelligence agencies."<sup id="cite_ref-284" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-284">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Politicians and human rights activists urged Theresa May's government to vote against Saudi Arabian retention of the membership of the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Rights_Council" title="United Nations Human Rights Council">UN Human Rights Council</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-285" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-285">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-286" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-286">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Amnesty_International" title="Amnesty International">Amnesty International</a>'s UK Foreign Policy Programme Director Polly Truscott said: "Rather than turning a blind eye to Saudi Arabia's continuing bully tactics, the UK should publicly hold the Saudi authorities to account for its appalling human rights record and the ongoing <a href="/wiki/Allegations_of_Saudi_war_crimes_in_Yemen" class="mw-redirect" title="Allegations of Saudi war crimes in Yemen">war crimes in Yemen</a> and should stop selling weapons to Saudi as a matter of urgency."<sup id="cite_ref-287" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-287">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup> May defended selling arms to Saudi Arabia stating that close ties with the country "keep people on the streets of Britain safe".<sup id="cite_ref-288" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-288">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Economic_policy">Economic policy</span></h3>
<p>Prior to her premiership, May outlined plans to backtrack on the longstanding government plan to achieve a surplus by 2020, following the UK's <a href="/wiki/Withdrawal_from_the_European_Union_by_the_United_Kingdom" class="mw-redirect" title="Withdrawal from the European Union by the United Kingdom">withdrawal from the European Union</a>. With uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook, <a href="/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer" title="Chancellor of the Exchequer">Chancellor of the Exchequer</a> <a href="/wiki/Philip_Hammond" title="Philip Hammond">Phillip Hammond</a> has suggested that the government's <a href="/wiki/Autumn_Statement" class="mw-redirect" title="Autumn Statement">Autumn Statement</a> may be used to "reset" economic policy.<sup id="cite_ref-289" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-289">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2015, while May was Home Secretary, an 18% funding cut in the police force had taken place with the loss of around 20,000 police officers. Before the <a href="/wiki/Manchester_Arena_bombing" title="Manchester Arena bombing">Manchester Arena bombing</a> and after the <a href="/wiki/November_2015_Paris_attacks" title="November 2015 Paris attacks">Paris attacks</a>, she was warned by a <a href="/wiki/Manchester" title="Manchester">Manchester</a> senior police officer that the cuts in the force and <a href="/wiki/Community_policing" title="Community policing">community policing</a> risked terror attacks in the city due to the lack of resources to undertake proper intelligence and anti-terrorist measures.<sup id="cite_ref-290" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-290">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-291" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-291">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-292" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-292">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In May and Hammond's 2017 budget, continued government policies were confirmed regarding freezing benefits.<sup id="cite_ref-293" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-293">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May's government published a <a href="/wiki/Green_Paper" class="mw-redirect" title="Green Paper">Green Paper</a> in November 2016 which considered forcing companies to reveal the difference between what their CEOs are paid and what their ordinary workers are paid.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup> On 1 January 2019 new regulations came into force for UK listed companies with over 250 employees to annually disclose the ratio of their CEO's pay to the median, lower quartile, and upper quartile pay of their UK employees.<sup id="cite_ref-295" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-295">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Workers.27_representatives"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Workers'_representatives">Workers' representatives</span></h3>
<p>Before her premiership began, May said that she planned to have workers represented on company boards, saying "If I'm prime minister ... we're going to have not just consumers represented on company boards, but workers as well."<sup id="cite_ref-theguardian1_296-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-theguardian1-296">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup> May aimed to put workers' and consumers' representatives on boards to make them more accountable.<sup id="cite_ref-297" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-297">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Nils_Pratley" title="Nils Pratley">Nils Pratley</a>, a journalist at <i><a href="/wiki/The_Guardian" title="The Guardian">The Guardian</a></i>, wrote in July "Fundamental principles of Britain's boardroom governance are being rethought. It is a very welcome development. In the more enlightened quarters of the UK corporate world, they can see that boardroom pay has eroded trust in business."<sup id="cite_ref-theguardian1_296-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-theguardian1-296">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup> Workers' representatives it appeared, would have made UK companies more like those in Germany and France.<sup id="cite_ref-298" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-298">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup> May was accused of backtracking in November 2016 when she said that firms would not be forced to adopt the proposal, saying "there are a number of ways in which that can be achieved".<sup id="cite_ref-299" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-299">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Environment">Environment</span></h3>
<p>Following the impact of <i><a href="/wiki/Blue_Planet_II" title="Blue Planet II">Blue Planet II</a></i> in 2017, the May administration outlined plans to approve further green policy. A particular focus has been on plastic and its impact on the environment. In March 2018, May announced plans for a plastic deposit scheme modelled on a similar policy in Norway to boost recycling.<sup id="cite_ref-300" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-300">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="EU_and_Brexit">EU and Brexit</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1097763485"><table class="box-Expand_section plainlinks metadata ambox mbox-small-left ambox-content" role="presentation"><tbody><tr><td class="mbox-image"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="[icon]" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg/20px-Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg.png" decoding="async" width="20" height="14" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg/30px-Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg/40px-Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="44" data-file-height="31" /></a></span></td><td class="mbox-text"><div class="mbox-text-span">This section <b>needs expansion</b>&#32;with: details about Chequers plan and defeat of withdrawal agreement. You can help by <a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theresa_May&amp;action=edit&amp;section=">adding to it</a>.  <span class="date-container"><i>(<span class="date">February 2019</span>)</i></span></div></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>May publicly stated her support for the UK remaining in the EU during the 2016 referendum campaign, but did not campaign extensively in the referendum and criticised aspects of the EU in a speech.<sup id="cite_ref-Theresa_May_wants_you_to_stay_in_the_EU._Has_she_blown_her_chances_of_ever_being_Tory_leader?_301-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Theresa_May_wants_you_to_stay_in_the_EU._Has_she_blown_her_chances_of_ever_being_Tory_leader?-301">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Theresa_May,_the_anti-Boris_who_just_might_be_Britain&#39;s_next_PM_302-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Theresa_May,_the_anti-Boris_who_just_might_be_Britain&#39;s_next_PM-302">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> It was speculated by political journalists that May had sought to minimise her involvement in the debate to strengthen her position as a future candidate for the Conservative party leadership.<sup id="cite_ref-Theresa_May&#39;s_silence_speaks_volumes_about_her_leadership_ambitions_303-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Theresa_May&#39;s_silence_speaks_volumes_about_her_leadership_ambitions-303">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup> Some in David Cameron's ministry likened May to a "submarine" on the issue of <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">Brexit</a> due to her perceived indifference towards the referendum and the EU.<sup id="cite_ref-304" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-304">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In a leaked recording prior to the Brexit referendum, May said,
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r996844942"><blockquote class="templatequote"><p>I think the economic arguments are clear. I think being part of a 500-million trading bloc is significant for us. I think, as I was saying to you a little earlier, that one of the issues is that a lot of people will invest here in the UK because it is the UK in Europe. If we were not in Europe, I think there would be firms and companies who would be looking to say, do they need to develop a mainland Europe presence rather than a UK presence? So I think there are definite benefits for us in economic terms.<sup id="cite_ref-Guardian26/10/2016_305-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Guardian26/10/2016-305">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup></p></blockquote>
<p>May also said Britain was more secure as part of the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">EU</a> due to the European arrest warrant and Europe-wide information sharing among other factors. She said, "There are definitely things we can do as members of the European Union that I think keep us more safe".<sup id="cite_ref-Guardian26/10/2016_305-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Guardian26/10/2016-305">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May's public reticence during the referendum campaign resulted in tensions with David Cameron and his pro-EU team.<sup id="cite_ref-306" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-306">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-dw_307-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-dw-307">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup> Following the referendum and her election as party leader, May signalled that she would support full withdrawal from the EU and prioritise immigration controls over remaining within the single market, leading some to contrast this with her earlier remarks on the earlier economic arguments.<sup id="cite_ref-dw_307-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-dw-307">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup> She later went on to say before the <a href="/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2017 United Kingdom general election">2017 United Kingdom general election</a> that she would be willing to leave the EU without a deal, saying that "no deal is better than a bad deal. We have to be prepared to walk out".<sup id="cite_ref-lefigaro.fr_2017_308-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lefigaro.fr_2017-308">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Reuters_no_deal_2017_309-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Reuters_no_deal_2017-309">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK)" title="Liberal Democrats (UK)">Lib Dem</a> leader, <a href="/wiki/Tim_Farron" title="Tim Farron">Tim Farron</a>, said it was "disappointing that Theresa May lacked the political courage to warn the public as she did a bunch of bankers in private about the devastating economic effects of Brexit. More disappointing is that now she is supposedly in charge, she is blithely ignoring her own warnings and is prepared to inflict an act of monumental self-harm on the UK economy by pulling Britain out of the single market." <a href="/wiki/Phil_Wilson_(British_politician)" title="Phil Wilson (British politician)">Phil Wilson</a> for the <a href="/wiki/Open_Britain" title="Open Britain">Open Britain</a> group said, "It's good to know that privately Theresa May thinks what many of us have been saying publicly for a long time, leaving the single market would be bad for businesses and for our economy. Now she is prime minister, Theresa May is in an unrivalled position to act on her previous concerns, starting by putting membership of the single market at the heart of her government's negotiating position."<sup id="cite_ref-Guardian26/10/2016_305-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Guardian26/10/2016-305">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Put_It_To_The_People_March_-14,_London,_UK_(40484849683).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Put_It_To_The_People_March_-14%2C_London%2C_UK_%2840484849683%29.jpg/220px-Put_It_To_The_People_March_-14%2C_London%2C_UK_%2840484849683%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Put_It_To_The_People_March_-14%2C_London%2C_UK_%2840484849683%29.jpg/330px-Put_It_To_The_People_March_-14%2C_London%2C_UK_%2840484849683%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Put_It_To_The_People_March_-14%2C_London%2C_UK_%2840484849683%29.jpg/440px-Put_It_To_The_People_March_-14%2C_London%2C_UK_%2840484849683%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2200" data-file-height="1469" /></a><figcaption>Parade float created by <a href="/wiki/Jacques_Tilly" title="Jacques Tilly">Jacques Tilly</a> at a 2019 protest against leaving the EU<sup id="cite_ref-310" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-310">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>On 22 September 2017, May officially made public the details of her Brexit proposal during a speech in <a href="/wiki/Florence" title="Florence">Florence</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-311" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-311">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup> urging the European Union to maintain a transitional period of two years after Brexit during which trade terms remain unaltered.<sup id="cite_ref-312" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-312">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup> During this period, the UK would also continue to honour its budget commitments of about €10 billion per annum, and accept immigration from Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-313" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-313">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup> Her speech was criticised by leading Eurosceptic <a href="/wiki/Nigel_Farage" title="Nigel Farage">Nigel Farage</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-314" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-314">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup> The European Union's Brexit negotiator <a href="/wiki/Michel_Barnier" title="Michel Barnier">Michel Barnier</a> welcomed May's proposal as "constructive,"<sup id="cite_ref-september22_315-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-september22-315">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup> but said it also "must be translated into negotiating positions to make meaningful progress."<sup id="cite_ref-september22_315-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-september22-315">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May did not initially wish to give MPs a vote on withdrawal from the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a>.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2017)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> <a href="/wiki/Nicky_Morgan" title="Nicky Morgan">Nicky Morgan</a> stated "in 2016 MPs aren't asking for a veto but they do want a say and we hope the Prime Minister will remember her earlier words". <a href="/wiki/Anna_Soubry" title="Anna Soubry">Anna Soubry</a> and <a href="/wiki/Nick_Clegg" title="Nick Clegg">Nick Clegg</a> also called for more parliamentary involvement.<sup id="cite_ref-316" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-316">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup> In November 2016, the <a href="/wiki/High_Court_of_Justice" title="High Court of Justice">High Court</a> ruled in <a href="/wiki/R_(Miller)_v_Secretary_of_State_for_Exiting_the_European_Union" title="R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union">R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union</a> that parliament must vote on the decision to leave the EU but May appealed to the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Supreme Court of the United Kingdom">Supreme Court</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-317" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-317">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Nicola_Sturgeon" title="Nicola Sturgeon">Nicola Sturgeon</a>, Scottish <a href="/wiki/First_Minister_of_Scotland" title="First Minister of Scotland">First Minister</a> has joined the case as did representatives from Wales and Northern Ireland. Sturgeon felt that the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament" title="Scottish Parliament">Scottish Parliament</a> should also consent to the UK triggering of Article 50. She said she was not seeking to prevent England and Wales leaving but wanted to preserve Scotland's place in the EU.<sup id="cite_ref-318" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-318">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup> In the end the Supreme Court required a vote in the UK parliament.
</p><p>May was accused of not having a plan if Brexit talks broke down.  There were fears that if talks failed Britain could be left trading under <a href="/wiki/World_Trade_Organization" title="World Trade Organization">WTO</a> rules which it was feared by some analysts would seriously damage jobs and livelihoods in Britain and Europe. May's ministers repeatedly promised to walk away from a bad final deal but, it was argued by some commentators, had no plans for how to manage without a deal.<sup id="cite_ref-319" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-319">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Ivan_Rogers" title="Ivan Rogers">Ivan Rogers</a> described May's Brexit strategy as "an accident waiting to happen". He said completing Brexit was "guaranteed" to take a decade and alleged May's hopes of a trade deal made to order meant that instability in the next few months was "quite likely".<sup id="cite_ref-320" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-320">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In late October 2018, the National Audit Office claimed  that it was already too late to prepare the necessary Irish border security checks in the event of a No-deal scenario—a weakness that could be exploited by criminals.<sup id="cite_ref-321" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-321">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Put_It_To_The_People_March_-3,_London,_UK_(46727760684).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Put_It_To_The_People_March_-3%2C_London%2C_UK_%2846727760684%29.jpg/220px-Put_It_To_The_People_March_-3%2C_London%2C_UK_%2846727760684%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Put_It_To_The_People_March_-3%2C_London%2C_UK_%2846727760684%29.jpg/330px-Put_It_To_The_People_March_-3%2C_London%2C_UK_%2846727760684%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Put_It_To_The_People_March_-3%2C_London%2C_UK_%2846727760684%29.jpg/440px-Put_It_To_The_People_March_-3%2C_London%2C_UK_%2846727760684%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2200" data-file-height="1469" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/2019_People%27s_Vote_March" class="mw-redirect" title="2019 People&#39;s Vote March">2019 People's Vote March</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>On 5 February 2019, May gave a speech to business leaders in Belfast to address Brexit stating the United Kingdom's relationship with Ireland was closer than the 26 other members of the EU. She affirmed the government's "absolute" commitment to the Good Friday Agreement and stated that Britain would seek to have no hard border in Northern Ireland.<sup id="cite_ref-322" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-322">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-323" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-323">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>It was reported in 2020 that former MI6 operative <a href="/wiki/Christopher_Steele" title="Christopher Steele">Christopher Steele</a> accused May, while Boris Johnson was foreign secretary, of ignoring claims that Russia may have secretly funded Brexit. Steele accuses May's government of selling British interests short by not taking matters further: "In this case, political considerations seemed to outweigh national security interests. If so, in my view, HMG made a serious mistake in balancing matters of strategic importance to our country."<sup id="cite_ref-324" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-324">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In July 2020 the <a href="/wiki/Intelligence_and_Security_Committee_of_Parliament" title="Intelligence and Security Committee of Parliament">Intelligence and Security Committee</a> report on Russia was released. It stated that the British government and intelligence agencies failed to conduct any assessment of Russian attempts to interfere with the 2016 Brexit referendum. It stated the government "had not seen or sought evidence of successful interference in UK democratic processes". <a href="/wiki/Stewart_Hosie" title="Stewart Hosie">Stewart Hosie</a>, SNP member said "The report reveals that no one in government knew if Russia interfered in or sought to influence the referendum because they did not want to know". However, the report stated no firm conclusion could be ascertained on whether the Kremlin had or had not successfully interfered in the referendum.<sup id="cite_ref-325" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-325">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Feminism">Feminism</span></h3>
<p>In 2005, May co-founded the mentoring and pressure group <i><a href="/wiki/Women2Win" title="Women2Win">Women2Win</a></i>. This group and May's personal efforts have been credited with increasing the number of Conservative women MPs and with supporting them. In government she lobbied for improvements to maternity leave, and as Home Secretary she acted on <a href="/wiki/FGM" class="mw-redirect" title="FGM">FGM</a> and introduced a law on <a href="/wiki/Coercive_control" class="mw-redirect" title="Coercive control">coercive control</a>. However, she has been criticised for the financial cuts made by her government, which have been claimed to have had the greatest impact on poor and vulnerable women.<sup id="cite_ref-326" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-326">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-327" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-327">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-328" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-328">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Same-sex_relationships">Same-sex relationships</span></h3>
<p>In 1998, May voted against <a href="/wiki/Crime_and_Disorder_Act_1998" title="Crime and Disorder Act 1998">lowering the age of consent for homosexual acts</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-329" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-329">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup> May was also a supporter of <a href="/wiki/Section_28" title="Section 28">Section 28</a>, calling a failed repeal in 2000 to be "a victory for commonsense".<sup id="cite_ref-330" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-330">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup> She was absent for the vote when it was successfully repealed in 2003.<sup id="cite_ref-331" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-331">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup> She also voted against the <a href="/wiki/Adoption_and_Children_Act_2002" title="Adoption and Children Act 2002">Adoption and Children Act 2002</a> that allowed same-sex couples to adopt.<sup id="cite_ref-17_apology_332-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17_apology-332">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Beginning in 2012, however, May expressed support for the introduction of <a href="/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Same-sex marriage in the United Kingdom">same-sex marriage</a> by recording a video for the <a href="/wiki/Out4Marriage" title="Out4Marriage">Out4Marriage</a> campaign,<sup id="cite_ref-333" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-333">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> in which she stated "I believe if two people care for each other, if they love each other, if they want to commit to each other... then they should be able to get married and marriage should be for everyone".<sup id="cite_ref-334" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-334">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup> In May 2013, May voted in favour of the <a href="/wiki/Marriage_(Same_Sex_Couples)_Act_2013" title="Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013">Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Bill</a>, which legalised same-sex marriage in <a href="/wiki/England_and_Wales" title="England and Wales">England and Wales</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-335" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-335">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> In 2017, May apologised for her past votes while taking credit for helping advance LGBT rights within her party.<sup id="cite_ref-17_apology_332-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17_apology-332">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Post-premiership_.282019.E2.80.93present.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Post-premiership_(2019–present)">Post-premiership (2019–present)</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Clarke,_May_and_Duncan_2019.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Clarke%2C_May_and_Duncan_2019.jpg/220px-Clarke%2C_May_and_Duncan_2019.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Clarke%2C_May_and_Duncan_2019.jpg/330px-Clarke%2C_May_and_Duncan_2019.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Clarke%2C_May_and_Duncan_2019.jpg/440px-Clarke%2C_May_and_Duncan_2019.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5568" data-file-height="3712" /></a><figcaption>On the backbench between <a href="/wiki/Kenneth_Clarke" title="Kenneth Clarke">Kenneth Clarke</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sir_Alan_Duncan" class="mw-redirect" title="Sir Alan Duncan">Sir Alan Duncan</a> during the Saturday sitting</figcaption></figure>
<p>After leaving <a href="/wiki/10_Downing_Street" title="10 Downing Street">10 Downing Street</a>, May took her place on the backbenches, remaining an MP to "devote her full time" to her constituency of <a href="/wiki/Maidenhead_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Maidenhead (UK Parliament constituency)">Maidenhead</a>, <a href="/wiki/Berkshire" title="Berkshire">Berkshire</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-336" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-336">&#91;336&#93;</a></sup> In the <a href="/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2019 United Kingdom general election">2019 general election</a> she was <a href="/wiki/Maidenhead_(UK_Parliament_constituency)#Elections_in_the_2010s" title="Maidenhead (UK Parliament constituency)">re-elected</a> as the constituency's MP.<sup id="cite_ref-337" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-337">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 30 September 2019, May divulged, at the Henley Literary Festival in <a href="/wiki/Oxfordshire" title="Oxfordshire">Oxfordshire</a>, that she was "thinking about writing a book", saying "It has been suggested to me that people involved in significant events should write about them so historians can look back and see what those who were at the centre of events were thinking, why they took decisions and so forth". When interviewed, she admitted that she had not read her predecessor <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a>'s memoir <a href="/wiki/For_the_Record_(book)" title="For the Record (book)"><i>For the Record</i></a>. She also said she had "no regrets" over her political career.<sup id="cite_ref-338" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-338">&#91;338&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In May 2020, May criticised the <a href="/wiki/10_Downing_Street#Office_of_the_Prime_Minister" title="10 Downing Street">chief adviser to the prime minister</a> <a href="/wiki/Dominic_Cummings" title="Dominic Cummings">Dominic Cummings</a> when he broke <a href="/wiki/Dominic_Cummings#COVID-19_pandemic" title="Dominic Cummings">lockdown rules</a> during the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom">COVID-19 pandemic</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-339" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-339">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-340" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-340">&#91;340&#93;</a></sup> She abstained in the vote on the second lockdown in Parliament.<sup id="cite_ref-341" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-341">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May has been mentioned as a possible candidate to replace NATO Secretary-General <a href="/wiki/Jens_Stoltenberg" title="Jens Stoltenberg">Jens Stoltenberg</a> following his expected retirement in 2023. In June 2021, British Secretary of State for Defence <a href="/wiki/Ben_Wallace_(politician)" title="Ben Wallace (politician)">Ben Wallace</a> expressed support for a potential May candidacy, saying "she would be an excellent candidate."<sup id="cite_ref-342" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-342">&#91;342&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 13 July 2021, May was one of 24 Conservative MPs who voted against their party, defying the whip for the first time in 24 years, over the government's proposal to cut its foreign aid budget. She criticised the government, saying in an address to Parliament, "We made a promise to the poorest people in the world. The Government have broken that promise."<sup id="cite_ref-343" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-343">&#91;343&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-344" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-344">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-345" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-345">&#91;345&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May was critical of Boris Johnson after the publication of the summary of the <a href="/wiki/Sue_Gray_report" class="mw-redirect" title="Sue Gray report">Sue Gray report</a>, stating "either my right honourable friend had not read the rules or didn't understand what they meant and others around him, or they didn't think the rules applied to Number 10. Which was it?"<sup id="cite_ref-346" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-346">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-347" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-347">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>On 16 March 2022, Russia banned May from visiting the country over the <a href="/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine" class="mw-redirect" title="2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine">war in Ukraine</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-348" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-348">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In March 2023, May was reselected as the Conservative candidate for <a href="/wiki/Maidenhead_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Maidenhead (UK Parliament constituency)">Maidenhead</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Next_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="Next United Kingdom general election">next General Election</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-349" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-349">&#91;349&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In September 2023, the House of Commons official portrait of May by artist Saied Dai was unveiled.<sup id="cite_ref-350" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-350">&#91;350&#93;</a></sup> In a radio interview with <a href="/wiki/Nick_Robinson_(journalist)" title="Nick Robinson (journalist)">Nick Robinson</a> she said that her Brexit deal would have been better and that she regretted saying "nothing has changed".<sup id="cite_ref-351" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-351">&#91;351&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Personal_life">Personal life</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:PM_in_China_(39124067045).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/PM_in_China_%2839124067045%29.jpg/220px-PM_in_China_%2839124067045%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="124" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/PM_in_China_%2839124067045%29.jpg/330px-PM_in_China_%2839124067045%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/PM_in_China_%2839124067045%29.jpg/440px-PM_in_China_%2839124067045%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4928" data-file-height="2772" /></a><figcaption>May with her husband <a href="/wiki/Philip_May" title="Philip May">Philip</a> in China, 2018</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:St_Mary%27s_Church_and_graveyard.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/St_Mary%27s_Church_and_graveyard.jpg/200px-St_Mary%27s_Church_and_graveyard.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="149" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/St_Mary%27s_Church_and_graveyard.jpg/300px-St_Mary%27s_Church_and_graveyard.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/St_Mary%27s_Church_and_graveyard.jpg/400px-St_Mary%27s_Church_and_graveyard.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1619" data-file-height="1207" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/St_Mary_the_Virgin,_Wheatley" title="St Mary the Virgin, Wheatley">Church of St Mary the Virgin</a>, <a href="/wiki/Wheatley,_Oxfordshire" title="Wheatley, Oxfordshire">Wheatley</a>, where May's father was the vicar and where May married<sup id="cite_ref-352" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-352">&#91;352&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-A_Guide_to_the_Parish_Church_of_St_Mary_the_Virgin,_Wheatley_353-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-A_Guide_to_the_Parish_Church_of_St_Mary_the_Virgin,_Wheatley-353">&#91;353&#93;</a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>May has been married to <a href="/wiki/Sir_Philip_May" class="mw-redirect" title="Sir Philip May">Sir Philip May</a>, an <a href="/wiki/Investment_management" title="Investment management">investment relationship manager</a> currently employed by <a href="/wiki/Capital_Group_Companies" title="Capital Group Companies">Capital International</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-354" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-354">&#91;354&#93;</a></sup> since 6 September 1980.<sup id="cite_ref-355" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-355">&#91;355&#93;</a></sup> It has been reported that former Prime Minister of Pakistan <a href="/wiki/Benazir_Bhutto" title="Benazir Bhutto">Benazir Bhutto</a> introduced the two during their time at Oxford.<sup id="cite_ref-356" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-356">&#91;356&#93;</a></sup> May credits future Australian Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Malcolm_Turnbull" title="Malcolm Turnbull">Malcolm Turnbull</a> for encouraging Philip to propose to her.<sup id="cite_ref-357" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-357">&#91;357&#93;</a></sup> May has expressed regret that she and her husband did not have children.<sup id="cite_ref-I_was_probably_goody_two-shoes:_358-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-I_was_probably_goody_two-shoes:-358">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup> The Mays are passionate <a href="/wiki/Hiking" title="Hiking">walkers</a>, and they regularly spend their holidays hiking in the <a href="/wiki/Swiss_Alps" title="Swiss Alps">Swiss Alps</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-359" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-359">&#91;359&#93;</a></sup> May is also a <a href="/wiki/Cricket" title="Cricket">cricket</a> fan, stating that Sir <a href="/wiki/Geoffrey_Boycott" title="Geoffrey Boycott">Geoffrey Boycott</a> was one of her sporting heroes.<sup id="cite_ref-360" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-360">&#91;360&#93;</a></sup> She also enjoys cooking, and has said that she owns 100 cookery books. Philip has said that she "is a very good cook".<sup id="cite_ref-Stamp_BBC_2016_30-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stamp_BBC_2016-30">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-The_Straits_Times_2017_361-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-The_Straits_Times_2017-361">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May and her husband reside in the Thames village of <a href="/wiki/Sonning" title="Sonning">Sonning</a><sup id="cite_ref-362" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-362">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-363" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-363">&#91;363&#93;</a></sup> which is within her constituency.<sup id="cite_ref-364" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-364">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May is a member of the <a href="/wiki/Church_of_England" title="Church of England">Church of England</a> and regularly worships at church (usually at <a href="/wiki/St_Andrew%27s_Church,_Sonning" title="St Andrew&#39;s Church, Sonning">St Andrew's, Sonning</a>) on Sunday.<sup id="cite_ref-365" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-365">&#91;365&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-366" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-366">&#91;366&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-367" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-367">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> The daughter of an Anglican <a href="/wiki/Priest" title="Priest">priest</a>, Hubert Brasier, May has said that her Christian faith "is part of me. It is part of who I am and therefore how I approach things".<sup id="cite_ref-368" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-368">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May is known for a love of fashion, and in particular of distinctive shoes; she wore leopard-print shoes at her 'Nasty Party' speech in 2002, as well as her final Cabinet meeting as Home Secretary in 2016. On <i><a href="/wiki/Desert_Island_Discs" title="Desert Island Discs">Desert Island Discs</a></i> in 2014, she chose a subscription to <a href="/wiki/Vogue_(magazine)" title="Vogue (magazine)"><i>Vogue</i></a> as her luxury item.<sup id="cite_ref-369" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-369">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup> However, she has been critical of the media focusing on her fashion instead of her achievements as a politician.<sup id="cite_ref-370" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-370">&#91;370&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>May was diagnosed with <a href="/wiki/Diabetes_mellitus" class="mw-redirect" title="Diabetes mellitus">diabetes mellitus</a> of <a href="/wiki/Diabetes_mellitus_type_1" class="mw-redirect" title="Diabetes mellitus type 1">type 1</a> in November 2012. She is treated with daily <a href="/wiki/Insulin" title="Insulin">insulin</a> injections.<sup id="cite_ref-371" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-371">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following her husband's <a href="/wiki/Knight_Bachelor" title="Knight Bachelor">knighthood</a> in the <a href="/wiki/2019_Dissolution_Honours" title="2019 Dissolution Honours">2019 Dissolution Honours</a>, she has been entitled to be styled as Lady May.<sup id="cite_ref-372" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-372">&#91;372&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-373" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-373">&#91;373&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-thetimes.co.uk_August_2020_374-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-thetimes.co.uk_August_2020-374">&#91;374&#93;</a></sup> As of 2&#160;February&#160;2022<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theresa_May&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, May's listing on Parliament's website, her own website, and social media do not use the style "Lady May".<sup id="cite_ref-375" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-375">&#91;375&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-376" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-376">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-377" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-377">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-378" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-378">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As a former Prime Minister, May, with her husband, had a place of honour at the <a href="/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Elizabeth_II" title="Death and state funeral of Elizabeth II">state funeral of Queen Elizabeth II</a> on 19 September 2022.
</p>

<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Awards">Awards</span></h3>
<p>Prior to and since her appointment to Government, May has actively supported a variety of campaigns on policy issues in her constituency and at national level. She has spoken at the <a href="/wiki/Fawcett_Society" title="Fawcett Society">Fawcett Society</a> promoting the cross-party issue of gender equality. She is the Patron of <a href="/wiki/Reading_University" class="mw-redirect" title="Reading University">Reading University</a> Conservative Association, in Berkshire (the county of her Maidenhead constituency).<sup id="cite_ref-387" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-387">&#91;387&#93;</a></sup> Her activism has earned her a number of awards.
</p><p>She was nominated as one of the Society's Inspiring Women of 2006.<sup id="cite_ref-388" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-388">&#91;388&#93;</a></sup> In February 2013, <a href="/wiki/BBC_Radio_4" title="BBC Radio 4">BBC Radio 4</a>'s <i><a href="/wiki/Woman%27s_Hour" title="Woman&#39;s Hour">Woman's Hour</a></i> described her as Britain's second-most powerful woman after Queen <a href="/wiki/Elizabeth_II" title="Elizabeth II">Elizabeth II</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-389" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-389">&#91;389&#93;</a></sup> May was Home Secretary at the time, and the most senior woman in that government.
</p><p>In 2001 she was made a <a href="/wiki/Livery_company#Liverymen" title="Livery company">Liveryman</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Worshipful_Company_of_Marketors" title="Worshipful Company of Marketors">Worshipful Company of Marketors</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-390" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-390">&#91;390&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In September 2017, she was listed by <i><a href="/wiki/Forbes" title="Forbes">Forbes</a></i> as the second most powerful woman in the world, behind <a href="/wiki/Angela_Merkel" title="Angela Merkel">Angela Merkel</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-391" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-391">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
